sens: Woman disciple of Jesus in Joppa
She who is raised from the dead by Peter's prayer
G5000.detail: Tabitha is a Christian woman living in Joppa at the beginning of the Church. Her Aramaic name means "gazelle" (Dorcas in Greek). She is known for her dedication: she "was full of good works and charitable deeds" (Acts 9:36), making garments and helping widows. When she falls ill and dies, the disciples lay her in an upper room and send for Peter. He arrives, puts everyone outside, kneels down to pray, then turns to the body and cries, "Tabitha, arise!" (Acts 9:40). She opens her eyes, sees Peter, and sits up. This miracle of resurrection becomes a powerful sign: many people convert after hearing about Tabitha.
G5000.origine: Tabitha is an Aramaic name, the language spoken in Palestine at the time of Jesus. The word literally means "gazelle" (טַבְיְתָא in Aramaic), a graceful and light animal. The two forms of the name (Tabeiθá and Tabitha) reflect variations in the transmission of the text. Luke also reports her Greek equivalent, Dorcas, which means the same thing.
G5000.emploi: Tabitha appears only twice in the Acts of the Apostles, in verses 36 and 40, in the account of her resurrection by Peter in Joppa. She symbolizes the active believer in practical love towards the poor and the widows. Her story comes after the conversion of the centurion Cornelius and paves the way for the expansion of the Church to the Gentiles. The miracle draws the attention of many: "this became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord" (Acts 9:42). Tabitha embodies the fruit of the Holy Spirit in action — kindness, generosity, serving others.
G5000.portee: Tabitha shows that true faith is expressed through concrete works: it is not limited to belief, but "was full of good works." Her resurrection is not a personal glory, but a sign that leads others to believe. For the Christian reader, she reminds us that God sees and values humble service, silent help to widows and the poor, and that our life as disciples is never insignificant — it can become the place of a powerful action of God.

sens: Assigned position in an order or sequence
Group organized according to a hierarchical structure
Marked place in an ordered succession
G5001.detail:
1. The word designates the position occupied by someone or something in an established order. It is like a numbered place in a line: everyone knows where they stand. In 1 Corinthians 15:23, Paul speaks of the resurrection of the dead "in their own order" — each in their place in the order of a grand event.

2. It also refers to a group of people or things arranged together according to a hierarchy or military structure. In biblical times, it was a military term: a troop organized in formation, each in their place for the whole to function.

3. The word emphasizes the idea of an ordered succession, a ranking according to a pre-established plan. Nothing is chaotic or improvised: everything follows an established order in advance.
G5001.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "tássō" which means "to arrange," "to put in order," "to assign a place." This root is found in other religious or military terms in the Greek Bible. In Hebrew, this word often translates as "banner" (the standard of a troop) or other terms designating an organized formation.
G5001.emploi: This word appears once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 15:23, where Paul uses it to describe the coming resurrection. He explains that Christ is the first to be raised, then "those who belong to Christ at His coming" — each in their order, that is, in their place in the divine order of resurrection. It is a highly theological term that places the resurrection under the sign of order and God's plan, not of chance.
G5001.portee: This word speaks to the believer of a comforting certainty: the final resurrection is not a chaotic rush, but will be accomplished according to an ordered plan that God has established. It invites the Christian to see that he has a secure place in God's plans, and that everything will be accomplished "in its order," that is, with precision and justice.

sens: That has been established, determined in advance
That is set, irrevocable
G5002.detail:
1. The word describes something that has been established and arranged in advance, like a date or a specific moment: in Acts 12:21, Herod presents himself "on a set day" — this day had been publicly announced, everything was prepared for this solemn appearance. It is an immutable appointment.
2. The adjective applies to what is settled, resolved, with no possibility of change. When something is fixed, it cannot be modified: it is an established order, a decision that holds.
G5002.origine: The word comes from the verb "tasso" (τάσσω), which means "to arrange, to dispose, to order" — the basic image is that of putting things in place, arranging them in a precise order. The adjective "taktos" thus designates what has been arranged and established in this way. This verb belongs to a family of words that all evoke the idea of order and organization.
G5002.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 12:21. It describes the day when Herod Agrippa I presented himself before the people of Tyre and Sidon, dressed in his royal garments, seated on his throne, to address them. This appearance was a public event planned in advance — a solemn set day. The context shows that it is an important date, marked by royal pomp, and that this presentation had political and religious significance.
G5002.portee: This word reminds us that even events that seem grandiose in the eyes of men — the splendor of a king, his apparent authority — remain under God's control. The day set by Herod to shine before his subjects becomes, in reality, the day of his judgment: it is there that death strikes him, according to the following account (Acts 12:23). This invites us to meditate on the difference between the plans of men and the purposes of God.

sens: To be in misery, overwhelmed by difficulties and sorrow
To deeply feel one's unhappy condition, to be aware of it and distressed
To experience grief, mourning, distress
G5003.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the concrete experience of someone going through trials, deprivations, sorrows — someone who truly suffers, who endures life's difficulties. It is a state of misery and distress endured.
2. But it also carries the idea of being aware of this state, feeling it internally, and being afflicted by it: it is not just passively enduring, it is suffering from the heart. In James 4:9, God calls believers to "feel" their spiritual misery, that is, to truly recognize and lament their state as sinners.
3. It thus also means "to be in mourning," "to experience grief" — the inner pain that accompanies the awareness of one's miserable condition.
G5003.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "taláiporos" (miserable, unhappy), which describes one who works hard, who suffers from pain. It is an image of forced labor, fatigue, and affliction. The verb conjugated here expresses the action of living or being in this condition of misfortune.
G5003.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in James 4:9. James uses it when he calls believers to recognize their guilt and to be afflicted by it: he invites them to move from laughter to mourning, to turn their joy into grief. It is a call to sincere repentance, to true regret for one's sins. The context shows that it is about truly "feeling" one's moral misery before God, not just knowing it theoretically.
G5003.portee: This word reminds us that true repentance is not superficial: it requires us to fully recognize our condition as sinners, to feel it in our hearts, to sincerely lament it. Only by acknowledging and truly lamenting our spiritual misery can we turn to God with humility and find His grace.

sens: Painful labor, exhausting effort
Suffering, moral or physical distress
Calamity, imminent disaster
G5004.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes hard, crushing work — the effort that exhausts. It is the image of the laborer overwhelmed by his field, or the worker broken by his task. In Romans 3:16, the text speaks of "destruction and woe" on the path of the wicked: this woe is the exhausting labor that evil brings, the endless fatigue of sin.
2. It also signifies suffering in general: the state of one who endures distress, sadness, pain. It is the woe of a broken heart, of moral misery.
3. By extension, it is the calamity that approaches, the disaster — that which will cause suffering. In James 5:1, Jesus warns the rich to weep "because of the woes that will come upon you": he refers to the judgments and ruin that await them for hoarding wealth while oppressing the poor.
G5004.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek ταλαίπωρος (talaïporos), composed of ταλαν- (tel-, effort, burden) and πόρος (poros, passage, way). The image is that of a burden so heavy that it blocks the way: one cannot move forward. The Greeks used it to describe the work of slaves or extreme fatigue. In the Greek translations of the Old Testament, it often renders the Hebrew שֹׁד (shod), which denotes destruction, devastation.
G5004.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, always in a context of God's judgment. In Romans 3:16, Paul cites the Old Testament to show that all humans, Jews and Gentiles alike, are under divine condemnation — woe and destruction mark the path of the wicked. In James 5:1, the apostle addresses the rich who have built their fortunes through injustice: he calls them to weep and mourn over the calamities that will come. In both cases, woe is not an accident, but the consequence of sin and the logical outcome of divine judgment.
G5004.portee: This word reminds the reader that sin and injustice never go unanswered. Those who accumulate through oppression, who reject God, will reap woe — either in this life or in the judgment to come. James 5 invites the believer to see with eyes of faith: the rich who exploit the poor carry within them the seeds of their own ruin. It is a call to justice and trust that God weighs the hearts.

sens: In a situation of suffering and physical or moral distress
Worthy of pity, in a lamentable state
Spiritually unhappy, distant from God
G5005.detail:
1. The word first describes one who suffers, who endures concrete or spiritual misery. It is the state of someone oppressed by their circumstances or by their own condition. Paul cries out, "Wretched man that I am!" in Romans 7:24 upon discovering his inability to do good by his own strength.

2. It also characterizes one who deserves compassion because they have fallen into a pitiful and degrading state. It is a shameful situation, where one has lost the dignity or comfort they believed they possessed. The church of Laodicea thinks it is rich and in need of nothing, but it does not know that it is "miserable" (Revelation 3:17): it is unaware of its true spiritual state.

3. On a spiritual level, the word expresses the condition of one who is far from God, who does not realize what they truly lack. This misery is invisible to the eyes of the world; it is the poverty of the soul despite the outward appearance of wealth.
G5005.origine: The Greek word ταλαίπωρος comes from a root that evokes pain and difficult labor (τάλας = one who endures). It translates the Hebrew שָׁדַד (shaddad) which means "to devastate," "to lay waste." This etymology clearly illustrates the image: a miserable person is like a house devastated, ruined by trials or by their own sins. The word appears rarely in the New Testament, but it carries strong emotional weight, that of deep distress and an urgent need for help.
G5005.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, but in two key contexts: one revealing the awareness of inner misery (Romans 7), the other exposing a false self-image (Revelation 3). In Romans 7:24, Paul expresses his distress over his sinful condition before deliverance through Christ. In Revelation 3:17, Jesus reveals to the church of Laodicea its true misery despite its sense of material sufficiency. In both cases, the word captures a moment of truth: discovering or being confronted with one's true spiritual condition.
G5005.portee: This word teaches that true misery is not primarily a matter of material wealth, but of relationship with God. Paul uses it to express that without the grace of Christ, the believer is left to a humiliating spiritual impotence. For the Christian reader, this word reminds that only Jesus can deliver from this inner misery and that spiritual wealth comes solely from Him, not from our accomplishments or possessions.

sens: Which weighs or is worth a talent (unit of weight or currency)
G5006.detail: 1. A talent is a very high unit of weight in antiquity, equivalent to about 30 to 40 kilograms depending on the region. This word thus denotes something extremely heavy. In Revelation 16:21, it qualifies hailstones — "a great hail, each hailstone weighing a talent" — which emphasizes the terrifying and cataclysmic nature of this plague: giant, crushing ice chunks fall from the sky as instruments of divine judgment.
G5006.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew and Aramaic word "talent" (kikkâr), which first denotes a plate or disk (by the image of something that spreads out), and then becomes a unit of weight used for gold, silver, and precious goods. In Greek, the talent takes on the meaning of both a unit of weight and a monetary unit (a very large sum). The adjective talantiaios simply derives from the noun tálanton and means "which is of the nature or weight of a talent."
G5006.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Revelation 16:21. John uses it to depict the seventh plague poured out on the earth at the time of final judgment: hailstones of prodigious weight fall upon unrepentant humanity. The choice of the word "talent" — the maximum known weight — accentuates the image of a superhuman and divine catastrophe. It is a technical term, used once to magnify the scale of apocalyptic judgment.
G5006.portee: This word helps the reader to imagine the violence and physical reality of divine judgment at the end of times. Rather than simply saying "a great hail," John specifies that each hailstone weighs a talent, which forces one to envision deadly and massive stones — a tangible image of God's judgment that falls justly upon those who have blasphemed.

sens: A unit of weight used in ancient times
A large sum of money (gold or silver) equivalent to that weight
Figuratively: a gift, a capacity, or an ability entrusted to someone
G5007.detail:
1. The talent is primarily a unit of weight used in the ancient Mediterranean world to weigh precious metals, particularly gold. It is a very heavy weight, representing approximately 34 kilograms.

2. By extension, the talent refers to a very considerable sum of money, equivalent to that weight of gold or silver. In the parable of Matthew 18:24, a servant owes ten thousand talents to his king — an astronomical sum, impossible to repay. In Matthew 25:15, a master distributes talents to his servants according to their ability: five to one, two to another, one to the third.

3. In the parable of the talents (Matthew 25), the word takes on a very rich figurative meaning: the talent becomes the image of a gift, a capacity, or an ability that God entrusts to each person to make it fruitful. The servant who receives five talents gains five more through his work (Matthew 25:16-20), while the one who receives a single talent hides it in the ground out of fear (Matthew 25:24-25).
G5007.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and originally referred to a balance or a scale. From there, it was applied to anything that was weighed, particularly precious metals. In the Greek Old Testament, the talent translates the Hebrew word kikkar, which literally means "disk" or "round piece" — the image of a round ingot of metal. The figurative sense of capacity or personal gift developed from the concrete meaning of a sum of money.
G5007.emploi: The word talent appears 8 times in the New Testament, concentrated in the Gospel of Matthew. It is mainly found in Matthew 18:24 (the parable of the unforgiving servant) and especially in Matthew 25:15-28 (the parable of the talents itself). In these passages, the talent is initially a very high monetary unit, but gradually the text imbues the word with an allegorical meaning: the talents become the gifts that God entrusts to men. The faithful servant "makes use of" his talents and multiplies them; the unfaithful servant buries them out of fear. This parable has given the word talent its modern meaning in French: a personal gift, a natural ability.
G5007.portee: The parable of the talents teaches Christians that they are not passive regarding the gifts received from God. Everyone has received something — little or much — and each will account for what they have done with it. Inertia out of fear or selfishness is judged severely. This word invites the reader to discover the abilities that God has placed within them and to put them to service in the Kingdom, rather than wasting or burying them.

sens: young girl
female child at the age of puberty
G5008.detail:
1. The word refers to a young girl, a child who has reached or is approaching puberty. It is an Aramaic term that Jesus uses when he says to Jairus' daughter, "Talitha, arise!" (Mark 5:41): he addresses her with tenderness in her own language, the one she spoke.
2. By extension, the word can also simply refer to a female child, a girl in general, without a precise age connotation.
G5008.origine: The word is Aramaic — the language spoken by the Jews at the time of Jesus — and literally means "young girl" or "maiden." Its equivalent in Hebrew would be close to "talita." Mark reports this Aramaic word as Jesus pronounced it, without translating it immediately, which shows the importance the evangelist attributes to Jesus' words in their original language.
G5008.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 5:41, at the moment when Jesus raises Jairus' daughter, a synagogue leader, who was dead or dying. Jesus takes the young girl's hand and says to her in Aramaic: "Talitha, koumi" (Maiden, arise). Mark then provides the Greek translation of this phrase for his Greek readers who did not know Aramaic. It is a moment of great tenderness where Jesus speaks to the child in her own language.
G5008.portee: This passage shows that Jesus spoke Aramaic and addressed each person in their language, with particular tenderness. For the believer, it reminds us that Jesus knows our languages, our customs, our most humble realities, and that he speaks directly to us, just as he did to this child. It is also a sign of his power: his word brings back to life.

sens: A closed room inside a house, a private and secluded place
A storage room or pantry
A secret refuge, hidden from the eyes of others
G5009.detail:
1. An inner room primarily refers to a closed room in a house, isolated from the outside world. It is there that Jesus asks to pray in secret: "go into your room, shut your door" (Matthew 6:6), an intimate place where one withdraws away from noise and prying eyes.

2. The word can also refer to a pantry or an attic, a place for storing provisions and supplies. Luke uses it when speaking of the ravens that have neither pantry nor barn to store grain (Luke 12:24), for God provides for their needs.

3. By extension, it is a hidden, secret, and protected refuge. When false messiahs claim to be in "the inner rooms" — hidden places — Jesus warns not to believe them (Matthew 24:26), for what is whispered in secret will ultimately be revealed in the open (Luke 12:3).
G5009.origine: The Greek word comes from an ancient form ταμιεῖον, which referred to a storehouse or granary. Its root relates to the idea of "to pile up" or "to accumulate." The Hebrew חֶדֶר ("room," "chamber") conveys the same concept in the Greek Old Testament. The word has gradually specialized to evoke any closed and secluded space: first a storage place, then an intimate chamber, and finally a secret refuge.
G5009.emploi: The New Testament uses this word four times. Matthew uses it twice: in the Sermon on the Mount (6:6) for the intimacy of personal prayer, and in the eschatological discourse (24:26) to describe secret places where one might claim to find the Messiah. Luke also uses it twice: when speaking of the ravens' pantry (12:24), an image of hidden provision, and announcing that everything said in secret in the inner rooms will be proclaimed publicly (12:3). The word thus shifts between the idea of material reserve and that of spiritual secret.
G5009.portee: This word invites the disciple to recognize that God sees what is hidden, and that authentic prayer is made away from human eyes, in intimacy. It also reminds us that nothing done in secret will escape divine judgment: hidden words will be revealed. It is a call to sincerity and the fear of God, rather than to showiness and seduction.

sens: Arrangement, disposition of things or people according to a sequence or regular structure
Division of religious service according to an established rotation
Decorum, harmony in behavior and organization of an assembly
Category or hierarchical class, notably the priesthood
Function or dignity attached to a specific office
G5010.detail:
1. In the most concrete sense, the word refers to the way in which something is arranged or organized. Order can be a regular succession or an established plan: it is the idea of something that is done according to a pattern, a logical sequence.

2. Among the Jews and early Christians, order could also refer to the rotation of service: this is why Zechariah performed his priestly duties "according to the order of his division" (Luke 1:8) — each class of priests had its day or period to serve in the temple.

3. Order also signifies decorum, harmony in relationships and collective behavior: Paul urges the assembly in Corinth that "everything should be done decently and in order" (1 Corinthians 14:40), meaning with respect for propriety and without confusion.

4. In Colossians 2:5, Paul praises "good order" among Christians, marking the healthy organization and discipline of a living community.

5. In hierarchical or ecclesial language, order refers to a class, a dignity, an official function. This is why we speak of "the order of Melchizedek" (Hebrews 5:6 and following): it means a priesthood that belongs to a certain category or tradition, a priestly class with its own rights and rules.
G5010.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb τάσσω (tássô), which means "to place, arrange, dispose, assign." The basic image is that of arranging, placing in position. In Hebrew, particularly in the Psalms (110:4), the word translates a declaration or established order: God pronounces His judgment, which establishes a stable reality. Order is what results from a thoughtful and commanded organization.
G5010.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the New Testament, mostly in the epistles. It is first used to refer to the rotation of priestly service (Luke 1:8). In the context of the Christian assembly, it evokes organization and discipline: Paul returns to this in Corinth to avoid confusion (1 Corinthians 14:40) and praises order in Colossae (Colossians 2:5). Its major usage concerns the priesthood: Hebrews uses it six times to speak of the priesthood of Christ according to the order of Melchizedek (5:6, 5:10, 6:20, 7:11, 7:17, 7:21). This "order" refers to a type, a stable and recognizable priestly category, different from that of the Levites.
G5010.portee: Understanding that "order" is not a mere mechanism, but a harmony desired by God. For the life of the assembly, this calls for respect for structures and discipline: authentic faith is expressed in an orderly communal life. Above all, the priesthood of Christ "according to the order of Melchizedek" affirms its eternal dignity, superior to that of the priests of the Law: it inaugurates a new and definitive relationship with God.

sens: Of modest condition, without rank or wealth
Of little importance, of low dignity
Humbled, afflicted, in distress
Humble in heart, devoid of pride
Gentle, unpretentious in behavior
G5011.detail:
1. The word primarily describes a low social condition, the absence of power or wealth. In Luke 1:52, God "has lifted up the humble": those who are at the bottom of the social ladder, devoid of power.

2. It also applies to one who is of little importance or appears unremarkable: in 2 Corinthians 10:1, Paul describes himself as "humble in appearance."

3. The word can denote a state of affliction, of being brought low: in 2 Corinthians 7:6, God comforts "those who are downcast," those whom distress has humbled.

4. But in the New Testament, "humble" takes on a positive moral value: one who has a humble heart, devoid of pride. Jesus in Matthew 11:29 presents Himself as "gentle and humble in heart."

5. Humility thus becomes a virtue of the soul, a disposition to submit without pride. James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5 contrast the humble with the proud and establish that God "opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble."
G5011.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "low," of "humbling." In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses terms like "shafal" (low, humble) and "ani" (poor, afflicted) for the same concept. Several derived words express humiliation: being brought low, dejection. The image is that of a low position, either materially (lack of power) or morally (absence of arrogance).
G5011.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the New Testament, mostly in the epistles of Paul and Peter. In Luke 1:52, it refers to the poor and dispossessed whom God lifts up. Paul uses it for his own apparent condition (2 Corinthians 10:1) and to exhort not to aspire to high things (Romans 12:16). Jesus applies it to Himself in Matthew 11:29, which completely transforms the word: humility is no longer shame or weakness, but a spiritual virtue. James and Peter associate it with divine grace: God opposes the proud but grants His favor to the humble. The meaning thus shifts from the social to the intimate, from the visible to the disposition of the heart.
G5011.portee: This word reveals that true spiritual greatness is found in the humility of the heart, not in power or wealth. Jesus Himself claims this. For the Christian, it is an invitation not to seek appearance, prestige, or personal elevation, but to recognize oneself as small before God and others. Humility becomes the door through which God pours out His grace.

sens: Agitate physically a liquid
Disturb or frighten someone
Worry, preoccupy the mind or heart
Sow division or confusion in a group
G5015.detail:
1. In the literal sense, to trouble means to agitate water or another liquid. In John 5:7, the sick man waits for the "stirred water" of the pool when an angel troubles it to fill it with healing virtue. This is the primary physical image of the word.

2. The word describes the fright or upheaval that seizes a person. When the angel appears to Zechariah (Luke 1:12), he is "troubled" and filled with fear. Similarly, Herod is "troubled" at the news of the birth of the King of the Jews (Matthew 2:3).

3. To trouble can refer to an inner agitation, a disturbance of the soul or spirit. Jesus himself is "troubled in spirit" when he announces his betrayal (John 13:21), and he tells his disciples: "Let not your heart be troubled" (John 14:1), encouraging them not to let fear invade their hearts.

4. In a collective context, to trouble means to sow disorder or division among a people. False teachers "trouble" the Galatians with their deviating discourse from the Gospel (Galatians 1:7), sowing confusion and worry in the churches.
G5015.origine: The Greek verb ταράσσω comes from a primitive root expressing agitation and disorderly movement. It translates in the Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) several Hebrew terms such as בָּהַל (to be troubled, to hasten) and רָגַז (to tremble, to be indignant). The word always evokes a disturbance, whether physical or moral. Other forms of the same verb appear with prefixes (διαταράσσω, ἐκταράσσω) to reinforce the idea.
G5015.emploi: The verb appears 18 times in the New Testament, primarily in the four Gospels and in Acts. In the physical sense, it denotes the agitation of water (John 5:4, 5:7). In the emotional sense, it describes fear or worry: fright at an angelic or divine appearance (Luke 1:12, Matthew 14:26), the turmoil of Jesus' heart in the face of his passion (John 13:21). The disciples are also troubled by events and fears (John 14:27). In the doctrinal sense, the verb is used to describe false teachers who sow division in the churches (Acts 15:24, Galatians 1:7, Galatians 5:10), or who agitate a crowd (Acts 17:8, 17:13).
G5015.portee: This word invites the Christian to recognize where their troubles come from: sometimes from fear in the face of divine mysteries, sometimes from worry about the future, sometimes from false doctrines or confusion sown by others. The repetition of Jesus' call "Let not your heart be troubled" (John 14:1, 14:27) offers the believer a response: trust in God and His Word calms inner turmoil. The word reminds that the Christian must remain vigilant against what seeks to disturb their faith.

sens: Agitation and confusion of water
Emotion, worry that stirs the soul
Tumult, public disorder
G5016.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes the agitated movement of water, as when it is stirred. John 5:4 speaks of the troubling of the water at Bethesda, this agitation marking the divine manifestation. 2. By extension, it describes inner agitation, the emotion that stirs a person from within — a trouble of the soul, of the spirit, similar to the movement of water. 3. In a collective sense, it can also refer to the tumult and disorder in a community or city, the agitation caused by fear or revolt (Mark 13:8 mentions the troubles that will accompany the last days).
G5016.origine: The word comes from the verb tarassô, which means "to stir, agitate, trouble." The basic image is that of water being stirred, or a mass of people being shaken. The Greek word translates Hebrew terms like "méhuma" (confusion) or "khala" (sickness), showing that Greek captures the Hebrew idea of a disturbance, whether physical or moral.
G5016.emploi: The word appears twice in the provided New Testament. In John 5:4, it denotes the troubling of the water of the pool of Bethesda, the visible sign of the angel's passage. In Mark 13:8, in the apocalyptic context, it speaks of the troubles (wars, famines) that precede the end, where it can be plural to denote several successive tumults. Each time, the trouble is a sign, a visible manifestation of a greater reality — divine or eschatological.
G5016.portee: This word reminds that trouble, whether physical or emotional, is never neutral in the Bible: it can reveal the action of God (as at Bethesda) or announce changes to come. For the believer, recognizing the troubles of the world — fears, disorders — as signs of the unfolding divine plan helps to maintain hope even in the midst of agitation.

sens: Disordered movement, confused and tumultuous noise
State of trouble and mental confusion
Riot, popular uprising
G5017.detail:
1. The word first evokes a chaotic physical movement, a noisy disorder: when Peter miraculously escapes from prison, "the soldiers were in great agitation" (Acts 12:18), frantically trying to understand what happened.
2. It also describes the inner state of confusion and deep trouble that seizes a community: in Ephesus, "a great trouble" arises "about the way of the Lord" (Acts 19:23), when the craftsmen fear for their business of making statues of the goddess Diana.
3. More broadly, it refers to social disorder itself, the collective agitation that can degenerate into riot or rebellion.
G5017.origine: The word comes from the verb "tarassô" (ταράσσω), which means "to trouble, shake, agitate." In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew "méhûmâ," which denotes confusion, chaos, or tumult. It is a later form of the word "tarachè" (ταραχή), which carries the same meaning. The root evokes the idea of a jolt that disturbs the normal order of things.
G5017.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the book of Acts. In Acts 12:18, it qualifies the material and mental confusion of the guards who discover Peter's miraculous escape. In Acts 19:23, it depicts the social and religious tumult provoked in Ephesus by the refusal of converts to buy the statues of Diana, troubling the prosperity of those who lived off it. In both cases, the agitation arises from an event that suddenly creates disorder and uncertainty.
G5017.portee: The word shows how the Christian faith and the presence of God can create trouble in the world. This should not frighten the believer: the apparent disorder of carnal minds in the face of the truth of the Gospel is a sign that God is at work. It also invites one to seek peace in Christ rather than to be swept away by the agitation of the world.

sens: originating or native to Tarsus
related to the city of Tarsus in Cilicia
G5018.detail:
1. Tarsus refers to a person originating from Tarsus, a large city in the region of Cilicia (in present-day Turkey). It is an adjective used to identify someone by their city of origin, similar to saying "a person from Lyon" or "a Parisian." Paul himself presents this way: "I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia" (Acts 21:39), affirming his belonging to this renowned city.
2. The word can also refer to anything related to or characteristic of Tarsus, its culture, citizenship, or features.
G5018.origine: The Greek word Tarseus comes directly from the name of the city Tarsós, the capital of Cilicia, a famous commercial and cultural center of antiquity. The Greek suffix -eus (as in "Philippos" or "Athenian") creates an adjective or noun designating the inhabitant or native of a place. Tarsus was an important city, which Paul emphasizes by calling it a "city that is not without importance."
G5018.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both times referring to Paul (Saul). In Acts 9:11, Ananias is instructed to find "Saul of Tarsus" at Judas's house after his conversion. In Acts 21:39, Paul himself introduces himself to the Roman tribune by affirming his Tarsian citizenship, showing that his origin from this great city grants him a respectable status. The use of the term highlights Paul's identity and pedigree before his apostleship.
G5018.portee: Paul proudly claims his Tarsian origin: it testifies that the Gospel has taken root in him, a man from a great Hellenized city. This reminds the reader that God calls people from all backgrounds, including educated and well-born citizens of great cities. It is a detail that humanizes the apostle and shows that his education and civic status did not prevent him from becoming one of Christ's greatest servants.

sens: Port city of Cilicia, in Asia Minor
Birthplace of the apostle Paul
G5019.detail:
1. Tarsus is an important city in Cilicia (region in southern Asia Minor, present-day coastal Turkey). It is a river port located on the Cydnus River, a commercial and cultural center where Greek civilization meets Eastern traditions. Paul was born and raised in this cosmopolitan urban context.
2. It is the birthplace of Saul, who becomes the apostle Paul. After his conversion and difficult beginnings in Jerusalem, Paul retreats to Tarsus (Acts 9:30), where he remains until Barnabas brings him back to Antioch for ministry (Acts 11:25). Paul himself recalls that he is "born in Tarsus of Cilicia" (Acts 22:3), marking this city as the starting point of his life before his apostolic calling.
G5019.origine: The Greek name Tarsos designates this famous port city. Tarsus was known in antiquity as a hub of commerce, philosophy, and learning: it is in Tarsus that Paul likely acquired his Greek education and urban culture before receiving religious training under the master Gamaliel in Jerusalem.
G5019.emploi: Tarsus appears three times in the Acts of the Apostles, always in connection with the apostle Paul. After his escape from Jerusalem, the brothers send Paul to Tarsus to protect him from his enemies (Acts 9:30). Later, Barnabas goes there to fetch him to associate him with his ministry in Antioch (Acts 11:25). Finally, Paul himself mentions Tarsus in his defense speech in Jerusalem to establish his origins and legitimacy (Acts 22:3). The city serves as a place of retreat, refuge, and starting point for the great apostolic ministry.
G5019.portee: Tarsus reminds us that God uses lives rooted in urban and cultured contexts. The apostle Paul, born in this great Greek city, received an intellectual and multicultural education that God transformed for the expansion of the Gospel. The mention of Tarsus also emphasizes that Paul's radical conversion did not erase his heritage but redirected it toward a divine purpose.

sens: To throw someone into the underground abyss where evil spirits are punished
To inflict eternal punishment on the powers of evil
G5020.detail:
1. The verb evokes the action of casting down, violently throwing downward — a forced fall into the depths. It refers to the underground abyss where, according to Greco-Hebrew beliefs, rebellious spirits, particularly fallen angels, dwell in anticipation of final judgment (2 Peter 2:4). It is a place of torment and separation from God, referred to here as "darkness."
2. Figuratively, the word expresses punishment and definitive condemnation: not sparing those who rebel against God, but subjecting them to relentless judgment. The image of the dark abyss symbolizes perdition and rupture from salvation.
G5020.origine: The Greek word comes from the name Tartarus, which in Greek mythology designates the deepest abyss of the afterlife, separated from ordinary Hades: it is the prison of fallen gods. Biblical authors take up this pagan image to reinterpret it in the service of revelation: the abyss becomes the place where God confines evil spirits. This is the only occurrence of this verb in Greek in the New Testament.
G5020.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:4, at the heart of the passage where the apostle Peter demonstrates that God does not hesitate to punish rebellions, even that of the angels who sinned. The example of the fallen angels is the first of three proofs that divine judgment reaches the guilty (the angels, Noah and his generation, Sodom and Gomorrah). The verb emphasizes the absence of mercy and the certainty of punishment.
G5020.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds a daunting truth: God does not tolerate rebellion, even among celestial beings, and no one can escape His judgment. It is a warning addressed to false teachers and wicked men of the time — they are not above divine law. This passage also invites vigilance: the grace of salvation is never acquired without responding to God's call.

sens: To place, assign someone or something to a location, a role, a task
To establish something, fixing it a place or a time
To predestine someone to a fate, a destiny
To voluntarily commit oneself to a cause or service
G5021.detail:
1. To designate a place or person for a specific purpose: it is to place someone where they need to be. Jesus "designated" a mountain in Galilee where his disciples were to meet (Matthew 28:16); a day or date is "fixed" for people to show up (Acts 28:23).
2. To establish an authority, giving it a role. The governing authorities have been "instituted" by God and derive their legitimacy from Him (Romans 13:1).
3. To predestine to a spiritual fate or destiny. Those who were "destined" for eternal life believed upon hearing the Gospel (Acts 13:48): the word suggests a prior divine arrangement.
4. To devote oneself to a service. The household of Stephanas "devoted" themselves to the service of the saints, showing a voluntary and dedicated commitment (1 Corinthians 16:15).
G5021.origine: The verb comes from military order: originally, it means "to arrange in formation, to place soldiers at their posts." Hence the broad meaning: "to put in place, to organize, to order." In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates Hebrew verbs that express the ordering or establishment of a reality: שׂוּם ("to put"), צָוָה ("to command"), נָתַן ("to give"). The meaning has enriched itself by moving from the military to the religious and personal.
G5021.emploi: Τάσσω appears 8 times in the given biblical usages, especially in Acts and the letter to the Romans. It first describes the action of fixing a concrete place or date (Matthew 28:16; Acts 28:23), then the establishment of an authority or order: Romans 13:1 affirms that existing authorities come from God and are instituted by Him. It also expresses divine predestination (Acts 13:48), where it can signify a prior design of God. Finally, in the middle voice ("for oneself"), it marks voluntary commitment or self-consecration (1 Corinthians 16:15: the household of Stephanas devoted themselves). The nuance depends on the context: divine command, earthly organization, or personal commitment.
G5021.portee: This word reminds us that the order of the world, particularly political authority, is part of a reality ordained by God. It also shows that spiritual destiny (eternal life) is linked to a divine design, not to chance. For the believer, τάσσω invites recognition of the order established by God and, personally, to freely "dedicate" oneself to His service, as the household of Stephanas did: an active commitment of the heart.

sens: Draft or sacrificial animal, male of the bovine species
Victim offered during a ritual sacrifice in the temple
Image of strength or raw power
G5022.detail:
1. The bull is the male animal of the bovine family, recognizable by its horns and imposing musculature. In the parable of the feast in Matthew 22:4, Jesus mentions the "oxen" that have been killed for a great meal: these are large butcher animals, symbols of abundance and generosity from the master.

2. In the Law of Moses, the bull was one of the main sacrificial victims offered at the temple. In Hebrews 9:13 and 10:4, the Apostle Paul reminds that "the blood of bulls" was presented to God for the ritual purification of the people, but he emphasizes that this animal blood can never truly take away sins — only the blood of Christ can achieve that. In Acts 14:13, the inhabitants of Lystra want to offer bulls to Paul and Barnabas, whom they take for gods come down from heaven.

3. The bull evokes untamed brute strength: it is the image of a power that knows no limits.
G5022.origine: The Greek word tauros comes from a very ancient Indo-European root and designates the same animal as the Hebrew word שׁוֹר (shor). All the peoples of the Middle East were well acquainted with this animal, essential for plowing and transport. The Bible uses this same word to speak of both the ordinary farm bull and the sacrificial bull of the temple.
G5022.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament. In the three passages from Matthew, Acts, and Hebrews, it always refers to a real animal: either the farm cattle that are fattened for a feast (Matthew 22:4), or the sacrificial animal (Hebrews 9:13, 10:4), or the cattle that are to be offered to false gods (Acts 14:13). Paul uses it mainly in his argument: he acknowledges that the bulls sacrificed at the temple had a recognized ritual value, but asserts that only Christ can truly purify sin. The context is always that of rituals, feasting, or visible power.
G5022.portee: The passage in Hebrews helps the believer understand why Jesus had to die: the animal sacrifices, however numerous and regular they were, remained powerless to take away sin. Only the unique and perfect sacrifice of the Son of God could do that. Meditating on the blood of the bull is to measure the insufficiency of our own efforts to reconcile ourselves with God, and to receive with gratitude what only Christ accomplishes.

sens: The place designated to receive a dead body
The act or ceremony of burying a dead person
G5027.detail:
1. A burial is a place dug into the ground or arranged to receive the body of a deceased person. It is a tomb, a grave. In Matthew 27:7, after the death of Jesus, the chief priests buy with the thirty pieces of silver "the potter's field, for the burial of strangers" — a plot that will serve as a cemetery for those who die far from their family.
2. The word can also refer to the act of burying a dead person, the funeral ceremony itself. It is the act of giving someone a grave and placing them there with respect.
G5027.origine: The Greek word ταφή comes from the verb θάπτω ("to bury, to place in the ground"). It is rooted in the concrete image of covering a body with earth. This verb and its derivatives appear in many funerary contexts in the Greek Bible, primarily translating the Hebrew קָבַר ("to bury, to inter"), which also expresses the action of entrusting a dead person to the earth.
G5027.emploi: The word ταφή appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 27:7. This unique usage speaks of the acquisition of the "potter's field" intended to serve as a burial place for the poor and strangers — that is, a public cemetery. The expression "for burial" shows that the main purpose of this acquisition was to have a suitable place to receive the dead. This passage also evokes the fulfillment of a prophecy from Jeremiah regarding the price paid for the field.
G5027.portee: The concept of burial carries spiritual significance in the Bible. Giving a decent burial to a dead person is to respect the body and honor the deceased — a duty of compassion and dignity. The fact that the religious leaders of Jerusalem bought a field to serve as a burial place for strangers shows that even the apparent rejection of Jesus led to an act of mercy towards the poorest.

sens: Place of burial, location where a dead person is buried
Tomb, structure built to house the remains of a deceased person
Image of death and decay
Representation of spiritual hypocrisy
G5028.detail:
1. The tomb is primarily the concrete place where a dead person is laid to rest. It is the location where the body of Jesus was placed: "Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb" (Matthew 28:1), the place where he rested between his death and resurrection.
2. By extension, it is a built tomb, a funerary structure. The Pharisees "build the tombs of the prophets and adorn the graves of the righteous" (Matthew 23:29), meaning they construct and embellish funerary monuments.
3. In the biblical image, the tomb evokes death itself and decomposition. Saint Paul cites the psalm: "Their throats are open graves" (Romans 3:13), comparing words of death to gaping graves that release corruption.
4. Jesus reproaches the Pharisees for being like "whitewashed tombs, which appear beautiful on the outside, but inside are full of dead men's bones" (Matthew 23:27): they have an appearance of purity, but their insides are filled with spiritual death and hypocrisy.
G5028.origine: The Greek word τάφος comes from the root θάν- (thanatos: death) and naturally designates the place of death and burial. It primarily translates the Hebrew קֶבֶר (qébher: grave, tomb). The term evokes the idea of covering, of burying: the tomb is the place where one covers and keeps the dead.
G5028.emploi: The word appears seven times in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in the Gospel of Matthew. It is encountered primarily in two contexts: first, the account of the passion and resurrection of Christ (Matthew 27:61, 64, 66; 28:1), where the tomb is the grave where Jesus was laid and from which he rose — it is the central point of the Gospel. Secondly, in Jesus' reproaches to the Pharisees (Matthew 23:27, 29), where the tomb becomes a symbol: the Pharisees are "whitewashed tombs," beautiful in appearance but rotten inside. Paul uses the image in Romans 3:13 (citing Psalm 5:9) to say that the corrupt words of men are like open graves.
G5028.portee: The tomb of Christ reminds the believer that Jesus truly lived, truly suffered death, and truly rose again: the resurrection is not a myth, but an event in history, validated by the empty tomb. The image of the whitewashed tombs invites every Christian to examine their heart: are we merely a beautiful appearance, or is our inner self transformed by the Holy Spirit? It warns against religious hypocrisy, which hides spiritual death under a guise of piety.

sens: Expresses a possibility, an uncertain supposition
Indicates hesitation or reservation from the speaker regarding what is stated
Suggests an intention or hidden design behind an event
G5029.detail:
1. The word expresses uncertainty: it is not known whether the thing has really happened or will happen. In Romans 5:7, Paul hesitates to assert that someone would be willing to die for a good man — he says "perhaps" to indicate that it is barely conceivable.
2. It is a discreet way of putting forward an idea without presenting it as certain. Philemon hesitates to interpret Onesimus' flight: "perhaps" he was separated for a divine reason, a hidden intention of the Lord. The adverb maintains uncertainty while raising the possibility.
3. In this context of Philemon, "perhaps" opens a spiritual perspective: what seems a misfortune could be a plan of God. It is less "I doubt" than "it may well be."
4. The adverb can also express a conjecture or a weak probability: it is possible, but not certain.
G5029.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective ταχύς (quick, prompt), which may seem strange for saying "perhaps." But the etymology reveals a logic: "perhaps" could derive from a notion of "quick conclusion" or "barely" (a common formulation in ancient Greek poetry). The word was mainly used in poetic literature before acquiring the weakened sense of "perhaps." In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses similar expressions to express uncertainty or possibility.
G5029.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, always in situations where the author expresses a cautious supposition. In Romans 5:7, Paul supposes that a person might perhaps be willing to die for a good person — but it is a barely conceivable supposition, hence the use of "perhaps" to temper the doubt. In Philemon 1:15, Paul interprets Onesimus' separation from Philemon as perhaps voluntary on God's part, a hidden divine intervention. In both cases, it is an adverb of modality that softens the assertion and expresses uncertainty or caution.
G5029.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us to remain humble in the face of what we do not understand: what seems a misfortune (like the flight of a slave) could be God's hidden design. "Perhaps" invites us to leave room for divine Providence and not to judge too quickly the events of our lives. It is also a lesson in rhetorical modesty: in matters of faith, apparent uncertainty can be wisdom.

sens: Without delay, rapidly in action
Without hesitation, soon
With haste, without thinking
G5030.detail:
1. The word expresses the speed of an action or movement immediately. When the angry master tells his servant to go "quickly" to fetch the poor (Luke 14:21), he asks him to hurry without lingering. It conveys the idea of prompt and diligent execution.
2. It also means "soon" or "in a little while," when speaking of a near future event. Paul announces that he will go "soon" to Corinth (1 Corinthians 4:19) or that he will send Timothy "soon" to Philippi (Philippians 2:19): it is a firm intention to come without much delay.
3. In certain contexts, the word carries a nuance of haste or excessive eagerness, even imprudence. Galatians 1:6 expresses astonishment that the Galatians have turned away "quickly" from the Gospel, suggesting a hasty and thoughtless turnaround, without weighing the danger.
G5030.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "quick, swift" (ταχύς), which expresses speed. In ancient Hebrew, it is mainly found alongside "מְהֵרָה" (quickly) and related forms. The root refers to the fundamental idea of movement without delay, of fluidity and swiftness.
G5030.emploi: The word appears about ten times in the New Testament, especially in Luke, Paul, and the pastoral epistles. In the Gospels and Pauline epistles, it first describes actions that happen quickly or upcoming arrivals: a servant running (Luke 14:21), a steward writing quickly (Luke 16:6), disciples hastening to the tomb (John 11:31). In Paul, it speaks of the delay before a visit: he will come "soon" if God wills (1 Corinthians 4:19). But the word also takes on a critical tone when Paul or Timothy speak of decisions made too hastily: the Galatians changed their Gospel "quickly" due to a lack of discernment (Galatians 1:6), and Timothy should not "quickly" lay hands on anyone without testing their worth (1 Timothy 5:22), which warns against thoughtless haste.
G5030.portee: This word invites the Christian to balance eagerness and caution. Being quick to obey, quick to serve (like the servant in Luke 14) is a virtue. But being quick to abandon faith, quick to judge without examination is a weakness and a danger. Speed is only good if it responds to a true and thoughtful command.

sens: That which happens or arrives with speed, without delay
That which is sudden, unexpected
G5031.detail: 1. The word describes what happens quickly, in a short amount of time. It conveys the idea of swiftness: Peter asserts that he will soon leave his body, "suddenly" (2 Peter 1:14), as if death could seize him at any moment. 2. The word can also depict what arises without warning, something unforeseen and harsh. False teachers bring upon themselves a "sudden" destruction (2 Peter 2:1): God's judgment comes unexpectedly, without giving time to prepare.
G5031.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek ταχύς (tachys), meaning "swift" or "prompt." It is a poetic and later form of the same word. The same root is found in other Greek words in the New Testament. The Hebrew מָהַר (mahar) conveys this idea of speed and urgency.
G5031.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 2 Peter. In these two passages, it qualifies eschatological realities: the death of the believer and the downfall of false teachers. In the first case, it emphasizes the uncertainty regarding the moment of death — it may come "suddenly." In the second case, it highlights the certainty of divine judgment which, although delayed, will come swiftly and without recourse. The word does not appear in other epistles or in the Gospels.
G5031.portee: This word reminds Christians of two essential truths: first, the vigilance regarding death, which may surprise us at any moment, and thus the importance of remaining in faith and obedience. Secondly, the assurance that God's judgment on evil will not be long delayed: false teachers will not remain unpunished for long. It is a source of confidence for the faithful believer.

sens: with greater speed, more quickly
in a shorter time frame, sooner
G5032.detail:
1. The word denotes an action accomplished with more speed, more swiftness than another. John 20:4 perfectly illustrates the meaning: "the other disciple ran faster than Peter," meaning he covered the distance more quickly. It is a comparison between two speeds.
2. It can also express the idea of an action that will occur in a shorter time frame, closer in time. Hebrews 13:23 illustrates this: "if he comes soon" means if he arrives shortly, sooner than expected. The emphasis is then on the time frame, not on the pace of the action.
G5032.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective ταχύς (tachys), meaning "swift, prompt." τάχιον is its comparative form: where ταχύς simply expresses swiftness, τάχιον establishes a comparison and means "faster." This is why it is always found associated with a comparison in classical Greek. The basic notion is that of swift movement, of speed.
G5032.emploi: This comparative word appears four times in the New Testament, always to express an implicit comparison. In John 13:27, Jesus commands Judas: "do it quickly," meaning without delay, in comparison to what would be normal. John 20:4 uses it for a physical action: John runs faster than Peter to the tomb. Hebrews 13:19 and 13:23 use it to express a temporal wish: to be returned to the recipient sooner, or to see Timothy arrive soon. In all cases, it involves a desired acceleration or anticipation.
G5032.portee: This word reminds Christians of the value of promptness and obedience without delay. Jesus does not simply say "do it" to Judas, but "do it quickly," emphasizing urgency and the absence of delay. For the reader, it is an invitation to act without procrastination in the things God asks, and to maintain hope that deliverance or reunion with brothers comes sooner than expected.

sens: The quality of that which is done quickly, without delay
The absence of delay, promptness to act
A short lapse of time, the imminence of an action
The speed of execution of a task
G5034.detail:
1. Swiftness is primarily a matter of speed: doing something quickly, without dragging. When the angel says to Peter, "Get up quickly," he commands immediate action (Acts 12:7). It conveys the idea of physical speed or urgency.
2. Next, the word denotes promptness, this quality of one who responds without delay. In Luke 18:8, the Lord promises to do "justice quickly," meaning without dragging out the matter.
3. The word can also carry the sense of time that is coming soon: in Romans 16:20, God will crush Satan "soon," meaning in the near and certain future.
4. Finally, it expresses the absence of delay in fulfillment: in Revelation 1:1, the things that "must soon take place" suggest a certain imminence, even if God's timetable exceeds our own.
G5034.origine: The word τάχος comes from a Greek root expressing the idea of speed and rapid movement. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb מָהַר (mahar), which means "to hasten" or "to make haste." This family of Greek words also includes the adverb ταχέως (tachéôs, "quickly") and the adjective ταχύς (tachús, "swift"), from which the prefix "tachy-" is known in French (tachycardia = fast heart).
G5034.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the New Testament, mostly in Acts and Revelation. In Acts (12:7, 22:18, 25:4), it expresses the urgency of immediate action: Peter must escape quickly, Paul must leave Jerusalem without delay. In Romans 16:20 and Revelation, the word takes on an eschatological hue: it emphasizes that divine intervention or the fulfillment of promises is approaching, even if they exceed our human timetable. In 1 Timothy 3:14 and Revelation 1:1 and 22:6, "soon" stresses the certainty and proximity of God's plan. Everywhere, the emphasis is on the absence of delay or the certainty of imminent action.
G5034.portee: This word reminds the believer that God acts without delay when He intervenes to save or judge. It also invites vigilance: the promises of Revelation, although their fulfillment exceeds our human calculations, are presented as near and certain. It is an exhortation to active patience and trust in God's faithfulness.

sens: Without delay, immediately, without lingering
Quickly, fast
Soon, in the near future
G5035.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is that of an action done "without delay": the women at the tomb depart "promptly" to announce the resurrection (Matthew 28:8), and Mary rises "promptly" when she learns that Jesus is calling her (John 11:29). It is immediate obedience, without hesitation.
2. The word can also simply mean "quickly," emphasizing the speed of the action itself: after a miracle, one may speak ill of Jesus "immediately" afterward (Mark 9:39), or an event occurs right away.
3. Applied to the future, "soon" expresses the proximity of an event: Jesus asserts, "I am coming soon" (Revelation 3:11) or threatens to come "soon" to judge (Revelation 2:16). The emphasis is less on speed than on imminence.
G5035.origine: The Greek word comes from an adjective meaning "quick, prompt" (ταχύς). It expresses the idea of speed and absence of delay. In Hebrew, the same concept was conveyed by the verb מָהַר (mahár), which means "to hasten." The family of the Greek word includes terms related to the notion of swiftness and immediacy, very common in the Greek language.
G5035.emploi: This word appears about 10 times in the New Testament. Matthew uses it to describe the hurried movement of the women at the tomb (28:7-8): they rise and run to announce the resurrection. John uses it for the promptness of Mary who rushes to Jesus (11:29). In Revelation, it is the preferred word to express the imminence of Jesus' return: "I am coming soon" (3:11, 22:7, 22:20). This repetition in Revelation emphasizes the eschatological urgency and the expectation of final judgment. The context thus shifts: eagerness in obedience and faith in the Gospels, urgency of Christ's return in Revelation.
G5035.portee: This word reminds the believer that faith calls for an immediate and unreserved reaction. The women at the tomb do not deliberate: they obey immediately upon hearing the announcement. But "promptly" in Revelation also carries a spiritual lesson: the return of Jesus is always presented as imminent, which should transform our vigilance and our expectation. It is not a matter of a calendar, but of a presence that can come at any moment.

sens: who acts quickly, without delay
who is done rapidly, in a short time
who comes soon
G5036.detail:
1. Prompt means one who acts or reacts quickly, without delay. It is the attitude of someone quick to action: James advises Christians to be prompt to listen to the Word (James 1:19), meaning to quickly put themselves in a listening posture. A prompt person does not linger; they decide and act.

2. Prompt also describes what is done quickly, requiring little time. When the father of the prodigal son tells his servants to bring the best robe quickly (Luke 15:22), he speaks of a rapid action, pressed by love.

3. Prompt can also mean that which is about to arrive, which comes soon. This is the sense of Christ's return: "Behold, I am coming soon" (Revelation 22:12), announcing a nearby event that is approaching.
G5036.origine: The Greek word tachus comes from a root that evokes rapid movement. It is the opposite of "bradys" (slow). In ancient Hebrew, this word often translates the verb "mahar" which expresses hastening, acting without delay. The family of the Greek word includes terms like "tacheos" (adverb: promptly) and compounds that reinforce the idea of speed.
G5036.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, in contexts where rapidity or immediacy are essential. Matthew uses it to urge reconciliation with one's adversary promptly (5:25), before the situation worsens. Luke places it in the mouth of the father who promptly orders the celebration to be prepared (15:22), revealing the joyful eagerness of his love. Acts speaks of joining someone as soon as possible (17:15), indicating an urgency of contact. James uses it for the inner disposition: being prompt to listen (1:19) is a spiritual virtue. Revelation uses it to affirm that Christ's return is imminent (22:12). The word thus expresses either rapid action or imminence.
G5036.portee: For the Christian, this word invites spiritual reactivity: to be prompt to listen to the Word of God, quick to obey, eager to reconcile. It also reminds us that Christ's return is near and that what comes from God often occurs with urgency and eagerness. It is a call not to linger in matters of faith.

sens: Links two words, two groups, or two phrases to unite them closely
Introduces a relationship closer than simple enumeration, especially in pairs or parallel listings
Emphasizes a logical or temporal connection between two elements
G5037.detail:
1. This small Greek word links two elements (nouns, verbs, phrases) like the conjunction "and" in French: it unites them to form a single thought. For example, in Acts 5:14, "men and women" refers to the entire community of believers: the word binds the two groups into a unity. In Matthew 22:10, "bad and good" enumerates the two kinds of guests in a single breath.
2. Unlike the conjunction καί ("and") which is more neutral and often simply enumerative, τε establishes a closer affiliation, a solidarity between what it links. It suggests that the two elements go together, that they form a pair or should be considered together. Acts 13:4: "Barnabas and Saul" — these two names are not simply juxtaposed; they designate companions on the same mission.
3. In constructions "τε... καί" or "τε... τε" ("both... and", "and... and"), the word marks a progression or coherent accumulation between the members. In Acts 19:12, "diseases left them, and evil spirits came out": the two effects follow as two sides of the same miraculous healing.
G5037.origine: τε is an enclitic particle (it attaches to the preceding word without receiving an accent) that Greek grammarians inherited from Indo-European. It functions like the Latin suffix -que in "magistratusque" ("and the magistrate"). It is also found in Italian "e" or in Old English. It has no true equivalent in classical Hebrew, but it often translates a simple juxtaposition of the Hebrew text, or reinforces the idea of conjunction when the Greek Old Testament needed to clarify the link between two elements.
G5037.emploi: τε appears 203 times in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in Acts (more than two-thirds of occurrences). It is rare in the Gospels, except in Luke. Biblical authors use it to link parallel enumerations, pairs of actors or actions, elements that should be seen together: the apostles and the disciples, signs and wonders, men and women. It can also structure a narrative by accumulating related facts: in Acts 1:1, "all that Jesus began to do and teach" links two aspects of a single mission. It is particularly frequent in narrative passages or dense enumeration, less so in argumentation or exhortation.
G5037.portee: For the reader, recognizing τε helps to see how Scripture groups realities: it does not juxtapose elements randomly, but creates meaningful pairs or sets. When reading "men and women," "signs and wonders," one understands that these elements go together, that they belong to the same movement of the Spirit or to the same divine intention. It is a discreet detail, but it invites the attentive reader to see the harmony and unity of what God is doing.

sens: Defensive structure made of stone or brick that surrounds and protects a city
Material limit, fortified boundary of a city
Image of divine protection and spiritual solidity
G5038.detail:
1. A wall is primarily a massive construction made of stone or brick, built around a city to defend it against enemies and intruders. It is a thick and tall structure, capable of withstanding attacks. When Paul escapes from Damascus, the disciples lower him "through a window, in a basket, along the wall" (2 Corinthians 11:33): the wall is the physical obstacle that must be circumvented to flee the city.
2. The wall delineates sacred or protected space: it marks the entrance and controlled access. In the vision of Revelation, the heavenly Jerusalem "had a great and high wall" with "twelve gates" (Revelation 21:12), signifying that only the elect may enter. The walls of Jericho, which "fell after they had marched around them for seven days" (Hebrews 11:30), embody a seemingly impregnable fortress that only faith in God can bring down.
3. The wall becomes a spiritual image of protection and stability: it represents the presence of God that surrounds and preserves His people, or the unshakeability of His eternal city. In Revelation, the wall of the heavenly Jerusalem has "twelve foundations" (Revelation 21:14) and is made of jasper (Revelation 21:18), a symbol of divine beauty and permanence.
G5038.origine: The Greek word τεῖχος (teichos) literally means what encloses or surrounds. It regularly translates the Hebrew word חוֹמָה (homah), which refers to the fortified wall of ancient cities. The Hebrew word comes from the idea of wrapping or encircling. Both Greek and Hebrew share this fundamental notion: a wall is what creates a barrier, a protective limit between the inside (safe) and the outside (dangerous).
G5038.emploi: The word τεῖχος appears nine times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in accounts of escape (Acts 9:25 and 2 Corinthians 11:33, where Paul leaves cities by climbing over the wall) and in the prophetic vision of Revelation (Revelation 21:12-19, where the heavenly Jerusalem is meticulously described with its walls). The context of escapes shows the wall as a real physical barrier that separates the inside of the city from the outside world. In Revelation, the wall becomes a cosmic and theological element: it protects the holy city, defines its boundaries, and bears the names of the founders of the Church (the apostles). The wall of Jericho (Hebrews 11:30) illustrates a wall that faith, not strength, can topple.
G5038.portee: For the Christian reader, the word wall reminds us that God's protection is never fragile: it is solid, high, impregnable—except by divine will. The walls of Jericho teach that seemingly insurmountable obstacles yield to obedient faith. The wall of the heavenly Jerusalem invites contemplation of the solidity and eternal security that God prepares for His people: no escape necessary, but a stable and beautiful city, forever preserved.

sens: Mark or manifest sign that establishes the certainty of something
Concrete and indisputable demonstration
Evidence that leaves no room for doubt
G5039.detail: 1. The word τεκμήριον refers to a mark or manifest indication, something that imposes itself on the observer as a certain reality. It is a concrete and visible sign that allows one to affirm with certainty that something is true. In Acts 1:3, the appearances of the risen Christ to the apostles over forty days are called "proofs"—tangible, observable events that strongly attest to His resurrection. 2. It is a demonstration that goes beyond mere testimony or word: it is concrete, visible, and verifiable. Jesus does not merely tell the apostles "I have risen"; He appears to them, speaks with them, shows Himself alive. These repeated appearances are proofs in the strong sense—facts that establish the reality of the resurrection without ambiguity.
G5039.origine: The word comes from the root τέκμαρ which means a mark, a distinguishing sign. In ancient Greek, τεκμήριον is used for what is "marked", observable, and therefore indisputable. It is a judicial and rhetorical term: the proof that the speaker opposes to the adversary to establish his case. The family of words is based on the idea of "marking" something in a visible and definitive way.
G5039.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 1:3. It is a deliberately chosen term to emphasize the compelling nature of the appearances of the Risen One. The Apostle does not say that Christ simply "spoke" to the apostles after His resurrection, but that He gave them proofs—concrete and repeated demonstrations of His being alive. These proofs include His physical presence, His appearance, His words concerning the kingdom. The use of the plural form ("many proofs") emphasizes the accumulation and coherence of these attestations, thereby reinforcing the certainty of the witnesses.
G5039.portee: This word reminds us that the resurrection of Christ is not an abstract doctrine or purely spiritual belief, but an event attested by observable facts. The forty days during which the risen Christ showed Himself to His disciples constitute tangible proofs of His triumph over death. For the believer, this means that the Christian faith rests on testimonies of concrete, verifiable facts, and not on speculation.

sens: A young child, very young
A disciple or believer regarded affectionately as a spiritual child
G5040.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a small child in the literal sense, at the beginning of life. It is a tender diminutive of the ordinary word for "child"—like saying "little" in French. The image is one of smallness, youth, one who needs protection and guidance.

2. In the New Testament, Jesus and the Apostle John use this word to address their disciples or the community of believers. It is not an insult, but a word of affection and authority from the master to his students: "My little children, I am with you for only a little longer" (John 13:33). This expresses that believers are like spiritual children to be formed, protected, and guided towards righteousness—"Little children, let no one deceive you" (1 John 3:7)—and that they must grow in true love (1 John 3:18).
G5040.origine: The word comes from τέκνον (teknon), which means "child" or "son" in a broad sense. The Greek suffix -ίον adds a diminutive and affectionate nuance, like the French suffix -on or -et: it expresses tenderness, intimacy, smallness. It is the same process as "house" / "little house" or "cat" / "kitten". The basic image is that of the child who is loved and whom one wants to protect.
G5040.emploi: This word appears 8 times in the New Testament, exclusively in the Gospel of John (once, John 13:33) and in the three letters of John (seven times). It is characteristic language of John. Jesus uses it to address His disciples at the Last Supper, signaling His imminent departure and the love He has for those He leaves (John 13:33). The Apostle John uses it in his letters to exhort the community: he calls all believers "little children", placing them under his pastoral care. The meaning remains constant: it is a term of tenderness mixed with authority, from the shepherd to his flock or from the master to his disciples. This word never applies to children in the literal sense in these passages; it is always a spiritual address.
G5040.portee: This word reminds the believer that before God and the apostles, he is like a child—dependent, learning, in need of guidance. Far from being humiliating, this address invites simple trust and filial obedience. Hearing it from the mouth of Jesus or John, the reader is enveloped in a paternal affection that protects him from deception (3:7) and calls him to grow in true love and righteousness (3:18). It is a word that creates intimacy between the master and the disciple.

sens: To give birth to children
To have descendants
To marry and start a family
G5041.detail:
1. To give birth means to bring children into the world, in the biological sense. It is the act of conceiving and delivering offspring. In 1 Timothy 5:14, Paul encourages young widows to "give birth," meaning to have children.
2. The word can also refer to the idea of having descendants and continuing one's lineage through children.
3. In the context of 1 Timothy 5:14, giving birth is part of a broader vision: to marry, have children, and manage a Christian household, which forms a coherent set of family responsibilities.
G5041.origine: The Greek word teknogoneō is composed of two elements: tekna (children) and gonē (generation, procreation). It literally means "to give birth to children." The root evokes the biological act of reproduction. This verb is relatively rare in the New Testament, indicating that the writers of the New Testament used other more common words to speak of motherhood or fatherhood.
G5041.emploi: The verb teknogoneō appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 5:14. Paul uses it in his pastoral advice to young widows: instead of remaining in widowhood, they are encouraged to marry and give birth. In this context, the term is not a simple biological description, but an exhortation to embrace married and family life as a path to stability and Christian fidelity. The word emphasizes the normalcy and value of motherhood in God's plan.
G5041.portee: This word reminds us that marriage and family are viewed in Scripture as blessings from God, not as obstacles to Christian service. For young widows in particular, Paul suggests that remarriage and starting a family provide a framework for authentic Christian living and protect against various temptations. This invites the modern reader to recognize the spiritual value of family and married life.

sens: The state of becoming a mother and bearing children
Fulfillment of the maternal function
G5042.detail:
1. The word refers to the concrete experience of motherhood, that is, a woman's act of conceiving, carrying a child, and giving birth. It is less about the general state of being a "mother" than about the action and process of bearing children.
2. By extension, it can also evoke the fulfillment of the maternal role in all its dimensions: raising the child, caring for them, and educating them. In 1 Timothy 2:15, the text states that a woman "will be saved through childbearing" — not that every woman must give birth to be saved, but that if she embraces motherhood with faith and virtue, she receives divine blessing.
G5042.origine: The Greek word is composed of two roots: "teknon" (child) and "gonia" (generation, birth). It thus literally describes the action of generating or producing children. This composition reveals the basic image: the coming into existence of a new life. The word is rare in classical Greek; Aristotle uses it when discussing issues of procreation and domestic life.
G5042.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 2:15. Paul addresses the role of women in the assembly and mentions the promise that a woman will find her salvation — not through teaching (forbidden in this passage), but by accepting her vocation as a mother with piety. The context is not to reduce women to motherhood, but to show that every call from God, accepted with faith and virtue, is a path of blessing.
G5042.portee: This passage invites believers to see motherhood not as a limitation or servitude, but as a blessed vocation from God. For women, it is a reminder that fulfillment can be found in the responsibilities entrusted by God. For all, it is an exhortation to honor the maternal role and the life that mothers impart. Motherhood with faith, charity, and holiness thus becomes a form of spiritual commitment.

sens: young person, boy or girl, from baby to adolescence
son or daughter, descendant
offspring, all descendants of a person
disciple or person being taught the faith
spiritual child, one who shares in the nature or qualities of someone else
inhabitant of a city or country
G5043.detail:
1. Child primarily refers to a young child, the little one: it is one who has just been born or is growing under the protection of their parents (Luke 1:7 speaks of Elizabeth and Zacharias "having no children"). The word evokes tenderness and dependence.

2. Child also simply means son or daughter in the parental relationship: this is the most common sense (Mark 10:29 mentions those who leave "house, brothers, sisters, mother, father, children"). Here the word includes children of all ages.

3. Broadly, child refers to offspring, all those who descend from an ancestor: Romans 9:8 asserts that "it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but […] the children of the promise."

4. The Bible also calls disciples or those being taught the faith children, as a form of affection from a teacher to their student: Jesus calls the paralyzed man this way (Matthew 9:2).
