5. Child takes on a figurative sense to designate one who shares the qualities or nature of someone: one is "children of light" (Ephesians 5:8) or "children of God" (John 1:12) when participating in their life.

6. Finally, the word applies to the inhabitants of a city or country: Jesus says to Jerusalem "your children" to refer to its inhabitants (Luke 19:44).
G5043.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to give birth, to bear." Its radical image is that of the newborn, of what has just been begotten. The Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) often links it to the Hebrew word meaning "son" or "child." It is a telling word that emphasizes the bond of filiation and dependence.
G5043.emploi: The word child appears 91 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew, Luke, and Paul. It primarily designates biological children in the literal sense (parents are advised not to provoke them, Ephesians 6:4; children who die in infancy, Luke 1:7). Very often it extends metaphorically: disciples are the children of the one who teaches them (1 Timothy 1:2, Titus 1:4), and especially, by grace, believers become children of God (John 1:12, Romans 8:16). Paul also uses the phrase "children of the promise" to show that it is faith, not physical birth, that makes us heirs of the promises made to Abraham (Romans 9:8). Finally, without any particular mystical sense, it designates the inhabitants of a city as its children (Matthew 23:37).
G5043.portee: This word invites the believer to two essential realities. First, being a child of God is not an innate status but a gift received through faith in Jesus Christ (John 1:12): it is entering into the family of God by grace, not by blood. Secondly, this filiation brings dignity and responsibility: one is an heir of God and a co-heir with Christ (Romans 8:17), which transforms our entire life. It is also a call to imitate the Father in His tenderness towards those we govern or teach.

sens: Nurture and educate children from infancy to adulthood
Carefully fulfill the maternal or parental duty
Demonstrate through this work a recognizable piety and faithfulness
G5044.detail:
1. The verb denotes the concrete action of raising, nurturing, and training children. It encompasses everything a mother or parent does daily: caring for, feeding, instructing, correcting, and preparing for life. In 1 Timothy 5:10, the text speaks of a woman who has "raised children" as tangible proof of her virtue.
2. It is an act that requires dedication, consistency, and patient love. The Bible values this ordinary task by listing it among good works: it is no less important than hospitality or serving the poor; it is part of it.
3. Raising children reveals a woman's heart and her commitment to God. This work becomes a visible sign of her faith, as it is within the family that the fear of the Lord is transmitted and Christian lives are formed.
G5044.origine: The Greek word is composed of "teknon" (child) and "trophē" (nourishment, education). The basic image is that of nourishing: providing the food that a small child needs. But the word quickly expands to encompass all education and training. Aristotle speaks of the raising of young bees. In Hebrew, the corresponding word in the Old Testament is often "qûm" (to keep, to raise) or terms meaning "to form, to instruct."
G5044.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 5:10. Paul describes the qualities of a widow who can be welcomed into the Church. He lists her good works: she has raised children, practiced hospitality, washed the feet of the saints, and helped the needy. The context shows that this is an ordinary yet precious work, a service that deserves respect and ecclesiastical recognition.
G5044.portee: This word reminds Christians that raising children is a holy vocation and a responsibility of great significance. It is a work worthy of recognition, both humble and fundamental. For parents, and mothers in particular, it is the assurance that their daily work pleases God and shapes the Church of tomorrow.

sens: Worker who works with wood to build or repair structures
Craftsman who makes or repairs wooden objects
By extension, any artisan specialized in precision manual work
G5045.detail:
1. The carpenter is a woodworker: he builds houses, roofs, frameworks, or repairs damaged wooden structures. It is a trade that requires skill and strength. In Matthew 13:55 and Mark 6:3, Jesus is referred to as "the carpenter," the son of Joseph: it was his family's trade in Nazareth.
2. More broadly, the word designates any artisan who works with wood or other solid materials using tools and techniques — joiner, sculptor, builder. The Greek word can encompass one who works with stone or metal, but the Segond specifically translates it as "carpenter," as this wood trade was well-known and esteemed.
3. Figuratively, the word evokes the working man, one who builds with his hands, far from idleness: a model of an honest and productive life, rooted in the reality of daily life.
G5045.origine: The Greek word τέκτων comes from a root that expresses the idea of "to make, to assemble, to build." It appears in several Greek contexts to designate any artisan of building or manual work. In Hebrew, the comparable word is חָרָשׁ (harash), which means "one who engraves, who shapes," and designates the skilled worker in various trades of wood, stone, or metal. The word τέκτων, while more specific to woodwork, represents the same dignity of craftsmanship.
G5045.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the Gospel of Jesus: in Matthew 13:55 and Mark 6:3. In both cases, it serves to identify Jesus by his social and familial origin — he is the carpenter, son of Joseph. This designation showed how the people of Nazareth viewed him: a man of the people, from a family of manual workers. It emphasizes not so much an admirable quality but a humble reality: before his public ministry, Jesus worked with his hands as a craftsman.
G5045.portee: That Jesus was a carpenter changes our view of his incarnation. He did not come as a wise man detached from the world, but by taking on flesh in the ordinary condition of a manual worker — sweat, fatigue, tools. This sanctifies humble work and the daily lives of simple workers. Jesus experienced real life before teaching; he rooted himself in the experience of his people.

sens: Who has reached its end, who is complete, whole
Fully developed, mature, adult (for a person)
Free from defect, lack, fully accomplishing its function
Entirely conforming to what it should be
G5046.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes what has reached its goal, what has gone all the way. It is the image of a completed race or a work brought to its fulfillment: thus, perfect love in 1 John 4:18 is the love that has fully deployed its power to cast out fear.
2. Applied to people, it describes one who has grown, who has reached maturity. Hebrews 5:14 contrasts it with the child: "mature men" can eat solid food, while the little child can only drink milk. It is spiritual maturity, the ability to discern good from evil.
3. The word also expresses the absence of defect, completeness without remainder. The "will of God" in Romans 12:2 is perfect because it lacks nothing, being good in every way. Similarly, the law in James 1:25 is perfect because it fully accomplishes its work of liberation.
4. In God and in the mature believer in Christ, this word denotes complete conformity to what ought to be: Jesus calls in Matthew 5:48 to be "perfect" as the Father is perfect, that is, to reflect his goodness and justice without rupture.
G5046.origine: The word comes from the root τέλος (telos), which means "end," "goal," "fulfillment." Something perfect is thus what has reached its end, what has realized its purpose. In Hebrew, it primarily translates שָׁלֵם (shalom, "whole," "unblemished") and תָּמִים (tamim, "without defect"), especially in descriptions of sacrifices or acceptable offerings to God. It is a word from the family of the Greek term "τελέω" (teleoô), to accomplish, and also appears in "τελειότης" (teleiotes), perfection.
G5046.emploi: The word appears 17 times in Greek, mainly in Paul and in the epistle of James. It carries two main nuances: on one hand, the spiritual maturity of the believer, who grows in knowledge and obedience (Ephesians 4:13, Colossians 1:28, Philippians 3:15); on the other hand, completeness, the absence of lack, in God, in Christ, or in his gifts (Matthew 5:48, Romans 12:2, James 1:17). James specifically uses it to exhort to endurance, which makes the work "perfect" (James 1:4), that is, fruitful, complete. In 1 Corinthians 13:10, Paul uses it to designate what is "perfect," the eschatological fulfillment, in contrast to the partial of now.
G5046.portee: This word opens for the believer a demanding yet encouraging vision: God does not call to an impossible perfection, but to a progressive maturity in faith, nourished by the knowledge of Christ and obedience. It reminds that every gift from God is complete, without lack or defect, trustworthy. Finally, it invites to discern that sanctification is a movement toward completion, toward the "perfect stature" of Christ, a call not to discouragement but to growth.

sens: State of complete accomplishment, without defect or lack
Completion, culmination of something towards its final form
Quality of one who fully and entirely achieves their goal
G5047.detail:
1. Perfection is the state of what is finished and complete, without any failure. It is the Greek word that denotes the total fulfillment of a reality in itself. In Colossians 3:14, the Apostle Paul says that love is "the bond of perfection": it unites all elements of Christian life into a harmonious and complete whole.

2. The word also evokes the idea of progression towards a goal, of culmination. In Hebrews 6:1, the text speaks of "pressing on to what is perfect": it is about progressing, growing spiritually until reaching complete maturity in the Christian faith, without returning to the elementary principles.

3. Broadly speaking, perfection refers to the fullness of what conforms to its essence and purpose: it is to be integral, total, without incompletion.
G5047.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective τέλειος (téléios, "perfect, complete"), which itself derives from τέλος (télos, "end, goal, fulfillment"). The family of this word revolves around the fundamental idea of reaching a goal, arriving at a conclusion, realizing the end for which something was made. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew תָּמִים (tamim, "whole, without defect") and תֻּמָּה (tumma, "integrity"), which also express the idea of completeness and absence of flaw.
G5047.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, which shows that it is a sharp and important notion. In Colossians 3:14, Paul lists Christian virtues (compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience) and asserts that love is the bond that unites them in perfection, that is, in a complete and functional whole. In Hebrews 6:1, the author encourages believers to advance toward perfection, understood as complete spiritual maturity, as opposed to remaining at the elementary level of the foundations of faith. In both cases, perfection is not an abstract quality, but a concrete state that one achieves or aims for as a Christian.
G5047.portee: This word reminds the believer that the Christian life has a direction and a purpose: to progress toward complete maturity and total fulfillment. Love is not an isolated feeling, but what binds together all spiritual life into a harmonious whole. The call to strive for perfection is not an impossible demand, but an invitation to continually grow in faith and relationship with God, without settling for the elementary foundations.

sens: Bring to completion, finish, achieve
Bring to maturity, make complete
Make perfect, without defect
Bring to its fullness (in speaking of a moral or spiritual quality)
G5048.detail:
1. To accomplish means first to finish an action or task: it is to bring something to its end. Jesus says, "The works that the Father has given me to accomplish" (John 5:36): it is about finishing the work that the Father entrusted to him. Likewise, on the cross, he declares, "It is finished" (John 19:28), meaning that the Scripture was fulfilled, completed.

2. To accomplish also means to bring something or someone to maturity, to its completed form. The works are not simply started, but brought to their fullness. This is why one can speak of "making perfect" in the sense of "completing".

3. In an ethical and spiritual sense, to accomplish someone is to make them morally and spiritually without defect, free from flaw. Christ was "made perfect through suffering" (Hebrews 2:10): his sufferings led him to the state of completeness and spiritual maturity that suited his role as Savior.

4. To accomplish a quality or feeling is to bring it to its maximum, to its perfection. When "love is perfected in us" (1 John 4:18), it fully fills our hearts and gives us confidence in the face of judgment.
G5048.origine: The word comes from the Greek τέλειος (teleios), which means "complete, finished, without defect". It itself derives from τέλος (telos), which denotes "the end, the completion, the goal". The word thus carries the image of reaching its goal, crossing the finish line. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew מָלֵא (malé, "to fill, to accomplish"), and תָּמַם (tamam, "to be complete, finished").
G5048.emploi: The verb τελειόω appears 23 times in the New Testament. It is very frequent in the Gospel of John (to accomplish the work of the Father) and especially in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where it describes how Christ was brought to perfection and how believers are brought to perfection through his unique sacrifice. In John, it is the action of completing a task or seeing the Scripture fulfilled. In Hebrews, it is first the path of Christ to his spiritual maturity through suffering, and then the result of Christ's sacrifice that makes believers holy "forever". In John's epistles, to accomplish love is to let it grow and flourish until its fullness in the believer's heart.
G5048.portee: This word reminds the believer that the work of Christ is not unfinished or imperfect, but complete. It invites us to see that God leads our lives to their fulfillment. It also shows us that we are called to grow spiritually and morally, to let our qualities and graces flourish in us until their fullness.

sens: In a complete manner, without restriction or lack
With totality and completion
Without reservation or partiality
G5049.detail:
1. The word describes an absolute completeness: nothing is missing, nothing is left aside. In 1 Peter 1:13, the Apostle speaks of an "entire hope", meaning a confidence that is not divided, hesitant, or partial, but rests wholly on the grace of God.
2. It is also the idea of a perfection brought to completion: the word evokes a total accomplishment, as when something is brought to its end without interruption or defect. The hope of the Christian is called to be "entire" because it must not be hindered by doubt or fear.
3. On a moral and spiritual level, "entirely" emphasizes the absence of inner division: the heart and spirit are not shared between multiple loyalties or fears, but are entirely oriented toward God and hope in Christ.
G5049.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective « téleios » (perfect, complete), itself derived from « télos » (end, accomplishment, goal). The root idea is that of a totality that has reached its end, which is not interrupted. This is why "entirely" carries the image of a flawless fullness and an achieved finality.
G5049.emploi: This Greek word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 1:13. Peter uses it to qualify the hope of the Christian at the moment when he exhorts his readers to sobriety and vigilance while awaiting the revelation of Jesus Christ. The adverb is chosen to emphasize that it is not a timid or shared hope, but a confidence that engages the believer in their entirety. It is a rare word, but its rarity underscores its theological significance.
G5049.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that faith can only be whole: it does not allow for half-measures or ulterior motives. Hope in Christ demands total trust, without division of heart. It is a call to inner sincerity and unreserved commitment to God.

sens: Action of bringing to completion
State of perfection, total completion
Full realization of a promise or expectation
G5050.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the action of bringing something to its end, perfecting it by completing it. Luke 1:45 provides a bright example: the angel Gabriel promised Zachariah that his wife Elizabeth would have a son (John the Baptist), and Elizabeth blessed Mary by saying that "the things which were told her from the Lord will have their fulfillment" — meaning that these divine promises will be fully realized, nothing will be lacking.
2. The word also evokes the state of perfection achieved when something is entirely completed, without defect or lack. In Hebrews 7:11, the apostle asks: "If perfection had been possible through the Levitical priesthood..."; he contrasts the imperfect perfection of the Levitical system (the perpetual sacrifices, never completed) with the complete perfection that only the eternal sacrifice of Christ could bring.
3. Broadly, it expresses the full satisfaction of an expectation, the moment when a divine promise or intention materializes without reservation.
G5050.origine: The word comes from the verb τελειόω (teleiōo, "to bring to perfection, to fulfill"), which itself is based on τέλος (telos, "end, term, goal"). This root evokes the idea of reaching the end, crossing the finish line. The Greek Old Testament often uses this word to convey the Hebrew notion of fulfillment and completeness, particularly in contexts of consecration and filling (as in Exodus 29:22, where it translates the idea of "filling" the hands of the priest — his complete investiture in his role).
G5050.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament: once in Luke and once in the Epistle to the Hebrews, indicating that it is a sought-after theological term rather than an ordinary one. In Luke 1:45, it emphasizes how the divine promises made to Zachariah and Elizabeth will be realized without flaw, illustrating the absolute reliability of God's word. In Hebrews 7:11, the author plays with its contrasting significance: the system of Levitical sacrifices could not achieve definitive perfection (offerings had to be continually renewed), while the priesthood of Christ according to the order of Melchizedek brings it once for all. These two usages converge: fulfillment = total and definitive realization.
G5050.portee: This word reminds the believer that God's promises are not empty or unfinished — they come to their conclusion with accuracy. For those who pray or wait, it invites trust: what God has said will come to pass. For the Christian, it also illuminates the superiority of Jesus' sacrifice: where the old rituals remained perpetually unfinished, Christ's work reaches a definitive perfection that fully satisfies divine justice. It is an invitation to rest one's faith on this total fulfillment.

sens: the one who completes, brings to its end
the one who perfects by leading to fullness
G5051.detail: 1. The one who completes: this is someone who brings a task to its end, who completes and fulfills it. The word suggests the idea of a race carried through to the finish, of a work brought to its perfection. In Hebrews 12:2, Jesus is called "the author and finisher of our faith" — he perfects it, he is its culmination.
G5051.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb τελειόω (teleiôô), which means "to make perfect, to bring to completion." This verb itself derives from τέλος (telos), which means "end, culmination, objective." The image is that of something reaching its goal, its natural end. The word appears only once in the New Testament, forging a unique expression to describe the role of Jesus.
G5051.emploi: This extraordinary noun appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 12:2. It is applied to Jesus Christ, who is presented as "the author and finisher of faith." This context suggests that Jesus does not merely initiate the faith of Christians: he leads it to its perfection, he fully accomplishes it. He is its culmination and the perfect model.
G5051.portee: This word invites the believer to contemplate Jesus as the one who perfects their faith. It is not an unfinished or fragmented faith that Christ inspires: it is a complete faith, brought to its spiritual maturity. This encourages fixing one's eyes on Jesus, who fully realizes what he calls us to live. It is a promise that our commitment to him has a destination, a fullness.

sens: Bringing to perfection (in reference to a plant or fruit)
Completing its natural development to the end
Bearing fruit or offspring that are finished and complete
G5052.detail:
1. For a plant or fruit, it is to bring maturation to its end: the seed germinates, grows, and ultimately produces a ripe and perfect fruit. The image evokes a natural process that goes all the way (Luke 8:14 speaks of the fruit that "comes to maturity").
2. It is to accomplish complete development, from beginning to end. Nothing is interrupted or left halfway: the plant or person reaches their whole and definitive state.
3. For a woman or female, it is to bear offspring to term, healthy and complete. The word applies to anything that leads a life to its normal flourishing.
G5052.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: τέλος (telos, "end" or "fulfillment") and φέρω (phérō, "to bear" or "to produce"). The initial image is therefore "to bear to its end" or "to bring to completion." It is a compound verb that emphasizes the idea of an action that does not stop midway, but goes all the way to its natural course.
G5052.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Greek Bible (Luke 8:14). Jesus tells the parable of the sower: the seeds that fell among thorns are choked by worries, riches, and pleasures of life, and they "do not bear fruit that comes to maturity." The context shows that this word denotes the complete accomplishment of a process: the fruit does not ripen, it remains unfinished. The image shifts its target (from the botanist to the soul of the believer), but the idea remains that of hindered maturation.
G5052.portee: This word speaks to every Christian about the necessity of allowing the Word of God to develop unhindered within them. Like a fruit that can only ripen if it is not choked, faith and obedience must grow without being blocked by the worries of the world. It is a call to cultivate a spiritual life that goes all the way, that bears finished fruit, not unfinished.

sens: to lose life, to cease living
to complete one's life, to reach the end of one's existence
to undergo death, to pass away
G5053.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to die, that is, to cease living: life stops, the body no longer functions. Herod dies in Matthew 2:19, and the centurion's servant is about to die in Luke 7:2.
2. The word can also refer to the completion of a life, its natural end: it is said that someone has fulfilled their existence and brought it to completion. David died according to Acts 2:29, which implies a complete life.
3. The idea of undergoing death as punishment or fate is also present: anyone who curses their father or mother will be punished with death according to Matthew 15:4, indicating a death inflicted.
G5053.origine: The Greek verb comes from a root that primarily means to finish, to complete, to accomplish (hence the notion of 'completing a life'). In biblical Hebrew, τελευτάω generally translates the verb מוּת (to die), which simply means to pass away, to cease living. Classical Greek already uses this word to mean to die, notably in Herodotus and tragedies. The notion of accomplishment underlying the word explains why a completed life is a dead life.
G5053.emploi: The verb appears 13 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and in Acts. It appears only once in an epistle (Hebrews 11:22 regarding Joseph who dies). It always refers to death in the real sense: that of a person (Herod, David, the centurion), of a situation (the woman with seven husbands in Matthew 22:25, each dying in turn), or that inflicted by law as punishment. In the parallel passages of Matthew 15:4 and Mark 7:10, τελευτάω translates the Hebrew from Leviticus when speaking of death as capital punishment. The word is a universal and natural term for dying, without any particular religious connotation.
G5053.portee: This verb reminds us that physical death is an inevitable fact of human existence in the current world, even for believers like Joseph in Hebrews 11:22. It invites the reader to consider their own death as the end of their earthly life, and thus to make good use of the time given to them. Finally, the Bible uses this word without dramatizing: death is not hidden, it is clearly named.

sens: The end of life, the passing of a person
The final outcome, the conclusion of an existence
G5054.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the moment when life ends, when a person dies. It is the concrete event of physical end. In Matthew 2:15, we speak of "the death of Herod": this instant when the king ceased to live, which allowed Joseph and Mary to leave Egypt and return to Israel.
2. More broadly, the word designates the conclusion of a life, its ultimate end — not only the moment of death, but the overall end of a human existence. This is why one can also speak of "death" as the necessary outcome towards which all life tends.
G5054.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb τελέω (to complete, to accomplish, to finish), which expresses the idea of reaching the end of something. It is the same root found in words like τέλος (end, outcome). Biblical Greek borrowed this word to translate the Hebrew word מוּת (death), particularly in the Greek translation of the Old Testament.
G5054.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 2:15, where Luke reports that Joseph and Mary remained in Egypt until the death of King Herod. This usage is quite literal: it simply refers to the moment of Herod's death, a historical event that marked the end of a threat to the child Jesus. Although rare in the New Testament, this word reflects the common Greek usage of the time to speak of passing away.
G5054.portee: This verse reminds us that even temporal events — like the death of a king — are part of God's plan. The mention of Herod's death is not just a historical detail: it is the moment when God allows the return of Jesus of Nazareth, thus fulfilling the prophetic promise. For the believer, the death of the powerful in this world changes nothing about the certainty that God governs history and accomplishes His purposes.

sens: To bring to completion, to finish what has been started
To fully realize, to execute or implement
To fulfill an obligation, to pay what is due
To come to pass, to occur according to a plan or a destined word
G5055.detail:
1. The most direct meaning: it is to finish, to complete an action or a discourse. When Jesus has "finished" His discourses (Matthew 7:28), He has completed speaking them; when He "finishes" the parables (Matthew 13:53), they are complete and fully spoken.
2. In a broader sense, it is to fully realize a task, a command, or a project: after the death of Jesus, His disciples "accomplished" all that was written about Him (Acts 13:29), meaning they saw all the prophecies and circumstances of His death come to pass.
3. It is also to settle a debt or obligation: one "pays" a tribute (Matthew 17:24) — to fulfill one's duty to the authorities (Romans 13:6).
4. Finally, when the word is in the passive voice or with a divine subject, it means "to come to pass" or "to be fulfilled": the written word "will be fulfilled" (Luke 22:37), or the power of Christ "is fulfilled" in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). It is then the word or the plan that comes to its intended conclusion.
G5055.origine: The word comes from τέλος (telos), which means "end", "term", "completion". The verb describes the action of bringing something to its natural or intended end. In the Greek of the Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb כָּלָה (kalah, "to finish", "to complete"), which shows that it is a well-established biblical word to express the idea of conclusion and fulfillment of divine purposes.
G5055.emploi: This verb appears 28 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and Revelation. In Matthew, it consistently marks the end of Jesus' major discourses (7:28, 19:1, 26:1), structuring the narrative material. In Luke and John, it takes on a strong theological nuance: "to accomplish" then means that the prophecies concerning Jesus are being realized (Luke 22:37, John 19:28, 30 — "it is finished"). In ethical context, the word expresses the execution of a command or obligation (Romans 2:27, Galatians 5:16, James 2:8). Revelation uses it to indicate that divine plans are coming to their conclusion (10:7, 11:7, 15:1, 17:17).
G5055.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God brings to completion all that He has started and promised. The "finished" words of Jesus invite us to receive them as complete and definitive. When Scripture "is fulfilled", it is a sign of God's faithfulness and the sovereign control He exercises over history. Finally, the call to "fulfill" the Law or a command challenges the believer to practical faithfulness, not superficial conformity.

sens: The stopping point or limit of an action, state, or period of time
The last element in a series or progression
The outcome, fate, or destiny that awaits someone
The tax or contribution that one must pay
The objective or goal that one aims to achieve
G5056.detail:
1. The end is the point where something ceases, where a period comes to a close. When the Bible speaks of "persevering until the end," it means holding on until the very last moment (Matthew 10:22). It is also the culmination of an action: "what concerns me is about to happen" (Luke 22:37) means that the fulfillment of what pertains to me is approaching.
2. Sometimes "end" simply refers to the last term in a list: Jesus claims to be "the alpha and the omega, the beginning and the end" (Revelation 21:6), meaning the first and the last, the one who encompasses everything.
3. The end can also be the fate or destiny of someone—good or bad. "Their end will be destruction" means that misfortune awaits them at the end of the road (Philippians 3:19).
4. When speaking of money, "end" means tax or tribute, the money that must be paid to the authority (Romans 13:7 speaks of paying tribute).
5. The purpose or hidden intention behind an action: "love is the end of the law" (1 Timothy 1:5) means that love is what the Law aims for, its ultimate objective.
G5056.origine: The Greek word τέλος comes from a root that evokes the idea of fulfillment and completion. In Hebrew, it often corresponds to the word קֵץ ("end," "term"). The related verb τελέω ("to accomplish," "to finish") and the adjective τέλειος ("perfect," "complete") share this same family: what is complete is what has reached its end, its total fulfillment. The central image is that of a limit reached or a destination arrived at.
G5056.emploi: The word is very common in the New Testament (41 occurrences). It is mainly used for "end" in the sense of completion: the end of the ages (1 Corinthians 10:11), the end of a trial (1 Peter 4:7), the end of a life (Luke 1:33: "his reign will have no end"). The Gospels frequently use it in Jesus' words about perseverance until the end of days. An important nuance: in Paul, the word can take on a nearly personified meaning—"Christ is the end of the Law" (Romans 10:4)—where it means less "term" than "that toward which everything converges" or "fulfillment." The sense of tribute or tax (Matthew 17:25, Romans 13:7) shows that in administrative context, it is a technical term of fiscal vocabulary. In all cases, the word carries the idea of an unavoidable limit.
G5056.portee: For the Christian, the word "end" invites one to think about life in terms of limits and objectives. Persevering until the end is not pessimism: it is recognizing that everything has a term and that faithfulness is measured by endurance. Christ being presented as the end of the Law, we understand that following Jesus means seeing fulfilled in Him all that God has aimed for from the very beginning. Reflection on the "end" of things—the end of trials, the end of this world—anchors the believer in the hope of a coming completeness.

sens: One who farms taxes and duties for the Roman administration
One who collects taxes and tolls in a given district
A man despised for his association with the Roman occupation and personal enrichment
A biblical symbol of the sinner to whom Jesus reaches out
G5057.detail:
1. A tax collector is primarily a tax farmer: he buys the right to collect taxes in a given area, in exchange for a sum paid to Rome. He enriches himself by collecting beyond the official rate. In Jerusalem, this means collaborating with the Roman occupier.

2. At the local level, he is a collector of taxes and tolls responsible for collecting taxes on roads and at city gates (like Levi in Luke 5:27). These subordinates work for the main farmer and collect money directly from merchants and travelers.

3. Tax collectors are socially cursed: associated with "bad characters" and prostitutes (Mark 2:16, Matthew 21:31), they are treated as notorious sinners. The Jews view them as traitors collaborating with Rome to enrich themselves.

4. In Jesus' teaching, the tax collector becomes an image of the sinner in need of mercy: Jesus calls the tax collector Matthew (Matthew 10:3), eats with tax collectors (Luke 5:29), and even places them before the righteous who will enter the Kingdom (Matthew 21:31). The tax collector in the Temple (Luke 18:10-13) embodies sincere repentance.
G5057.origine: The Greek word comes from two roots: "telos" (tax, duty) and "ōneōmai" (to buy, to trade). A tax collector is therefore literally one who "buys" the right to collect taxes. In Latin, he is called "publicanus," from which our French word "publicain" derives. This practice was common in the Roman Empire: the state rented the right to collect taxes to private entrepreneurs who profited by taking a surplus.
G5057.emploi: The word appears about twenty times in the Gospels, almost exclusively in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. It always refers to a tax collector under Roman rule. Matthew is the only apostle explicitly called a tax collector (Matthew 10:3), a former collector called to follow Jesus (Matthew 9:9-13). Tax collectors frequently appear in controversies: the Pharisees reproach Jesus for eating with them (Mark 2:15-16), which was considered a ritual defilement. Gradually, Jesus rehabilitates their image: he announces that tax collectors and prostitutes will precede them in the Kingdom (Matthew 21:31), and sets a tax collector as an example of true prayer and humility (Luke 18:10-13). The word carries a narrative arc from contempt to mercy.
G5057.portee: For the Christian, the tax collector embodies two essential truths. First, that no one is too sinful or too despised to be rejected by Jesus: Matthew's calling and the acceptance of tax collectors show that grace is extended to the most compromised. Second, that religious exteriority (like that of the Pharisees) is inferior to humility and sincere repentance: the tax collector in the Temple who "dare not lift his eyes" will pray better than the Pharisee who boasts. These images remind us that Jesus did not come for the righteous, but for sinners, and that there is no caste inaccessible to His love.

sens: Small cabin or building where taxes on goods and travelers were collected
Workplace of tax collectors, that is, Roman tax collectors
G5058.detail:
1. The toll booth is a small building, often a cabin, set up at a strategic location (road crossing, bridge, city entrance) where Roman authorities collected a tax on goods passing through or on travelers. It is a public building, visible, dedicated to tax collection: in Matthew 9:9, Jesus sees Matthew sitting "at the toll booth," that is, at the counter where he practiced his trade.
2. By extension, it is the workplace of tax collectors, these men whom the Jews viewed as collaborators with the Roman occupier. The three Gospels (Matthew, Mark, and Luke) describe the same calling of Levi-Matthew: he was sitting at the toll booth when Jesus met him and called him to follow, transforming this tax collector into an apostle.
G5058.origine: The Greek word τελώνιον comes from the word τελώνης ("tax collector"), which is itself formed from τέλος ("tax, tribute"). The suffix -ιον designates a place. The Greek thus conveys the idea of a house or hut related to the collection of Roman taxes. It is an administrative term, linked to the fiscal system of the Empire.
G5058.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the first three Gospels, during the same event: the calling of Levi-Matthew to his workplace. In Matthew 9:9 and Luke 5:27, it is translated as "toll booth" or "toll"; in Mark 2:14, as "toll booth." In each case, Jesus approaches a tax collector at his workplace and calls him to follow. The word emphasizes that Jesus' call reaches men in their ordinary jobs, even if they work for an oppressive system.
G5058.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus did not only call the pure or the religious: he approached tax collectors, collaborators of the Roman power, men deemed dishonest and unclean. The image of the toll booth embodies the ordinary secular, the place of foreign power and dubious gains. It is there that Christ intervenes and transforms a life. For the Christian reader, it is a promise: no job, no place, no man is beyond the reach of Jesus' call.

sens: Extraordinary event that evokes astonishment and fear
Supernatural act that manifests divine power
Miraculous sign that accompanies and confirms the preaching of the Gospel
G5059.detail:
1. A wonder is primarily an event that exceeds the ordinary laws of nature and provokes admiration: this is why John 4:48 places "miracles and wonders" at the heart of the faith of witnesses. The word evokes the idea of something out of the ordinary, that astonishes and disturbs those who observe it.
2. In the New Testament, a wonder is always an act that manifests divine power at work. In Acts 2:22, Jesus performs wonders, miracles, and signs "by the hand of God" — it is a supernatural act that shows that God is acting. Acts 6:8 describes Stephen who "was doing wonders and great miracles among the people."
3. The wonder serves as a testimony and confirmation to the word of the Gospel: in Acts 14:3, the apostles speak "supported by the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace by signs and wonders." It is a sign that accredits the apostolic preaching.
G5059.origine: The Greek word τέρας comes from a root that evokes the idea of what is astonishing, extraordinary. It generally translates the Hebrew מוֹפֵת (mopheth) in the Greek Old Testament, which also means a wonderful sign or omen. The wonder is always presented as the effect of divine power acting in history.
G5059.emploi: The word "wonder" appears 16 times in the New Testament, always in the plural (wonders and miracles, or wonders and signs). It is especially frequent in the Acts of the Apostles, which reports the miracles of the apostles and the early disciples: Acts 2:19, 2:22, 2:43, 4:30, 5:12, 6:8, 14:3, 15:12. Matthew 24:24 and Mark 13:22 warn that false prophets will perform great wonders to deceive the elect. John 4:48 criticizes those who believe only if they see miracles and wonders. Paul also mentions the wonders he performed in Romans 15:19 and 2 Corinthians 12:12. The wonder is always associated with divine power: it confirms the word and legitimizes the message of the apostles.
G5059.portee: For the believer, the wonder is not a spectacle to seek or a magical proof. Matthew 24:24 and John 4:48 warn that faith should not depend solely on miracles. But in Acts, wonders attest that God is truly acting through his apostles and validate the message of the Gospel. The wonder reminds us that God is never absent from his people and that he confirms his word through powerful acts.

sens: scribe who wrote the letter to the Romans under Paul's dictation
G5060.detail: Tertius is the name of the Christian who physically wrote the epistle to the Romans. Paul dictated his letter, and Tertius, probably an assistant or collaborator, held the pen to transcribe the apostle's words. At the end of the letter, Tertius inserts himself into the greeting addressed to the Romans, presenting himself as the one who "wrote this letter" (Romans 16:22), which shows his concrete role and place in the Christian community.
G5060.origine: Tertius is a common Roman name, literally meaning "the third" (from Latin tertius). His name may suggest that he was the third child in a family, a common Roman practice of numbering children this way. This name indicates that Tertius was probably a non-Jew or a Hellenized Jew integrated into the Roman world.
G5060.emploi: Tertius appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 16:22. Paul entrusts him with the important task of writing his major letter to the Romans. His intervention in the letter, where he greets himself, shows that the secretaries of the apostles did not remain in the shadows: they were recognized members of the Christian assembly, worthy of participating in the communal greeting. This also reveals the concrete process of composing Pauline epistles.
G5060.portee: The mention of Tertius reminds us that the epistles of the New Testament are true letters, written by concrete men from apostolic thought. It humanizes the process of revelation: God expresses himself through the voice of his witnesses, but also through the hands of faithful collaborators. It is an invitation to recognize the hidden workers of the kingdom, who serve without always being in the spotlight.

sens: Jewish orator who accused Paul before the Roman governor Felix
G5061.detail: Tertullus is a Jewish lawyer or orator who appears before the Roman governor Felix to present the accusations against the apostle Paul. His Latin name indicates that he is probably a Hellenized Jew, accustomed to pleading in Roman courts according to the rules of Greco-Roman eloquence. He represents the Jewish authorities (the high priest Ananias and the elders) who want to have Paul condemned.
G5061.origine: Tertullus is a Latin name (diminutive of Tertius) borne by a figure from Roman antiquity. Its use by Luke in Acts indicates that he is a professional from the Roman bar, probably a Jew from the diaspora who mastered rhetoric and Roman legal procedures.
G5061.emploi: Tertullus appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 24. He intervenes after Paul has been arrested in Jerusalem and transferred to Caesarea, the seat of the Roman governor. Ananias and the Jewish elders send him to present their case against Paul (Acts 24:1); Tertullus then stands up to accuse Paul and justify the request of the Jewish authorities (Acts 24:2). His role is that of a professional in Roman law tasked with convincing the magistrate.
G5061.portee: Tertullus illustrates the Jewish authorities' recourse to Roman institutions to persecute the Church. His appearance reminds us that early Christians had to face both Jewish religious hostility and the pagan judicial system. It is an opportunity for Luke to show how Paul, despite elaborate accusations, relies on his defense before God and the Roman magistrates.

sens: The whole number equal to four times ten.
A period of time, often symbolic or transitional, marked by trial or waiting.
A number of people or things counted.
G5062.detail:
1. This is primarily the literal number forty, the one that is counted: "After fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry" (Matthew 4:2). It is used to enumerate durations, measures, or specific quantities.
2. In the Bible, forty often becomes a number of testing or transition: the people of Israel wandered for forty years in the desert (Acts 7:30 and following), Jesus fasted for forty days in the desert before his temptation. These forty units mark a time when God tests faith and purifies his people.
3. The number is also used to count people or groups: "forty-six years to build this temple" (John 2:20), "one hundred forty-four thousand" bearing the seal of God (Revelation 7:4 and 14:1), or "forty lashes minus one" inflicted on the apostle Paul (2 Corinthians 11:24).
G5062.origine: The Greek word τεσσεράκοντα (tessarakonta) comes from an ancient Indo-European root and simply means the number four multiplied by ten. It follows the same constructions as other Greek numbers. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses the corresponding word (arbaʿim) exactly in the same contexts: the forty years in the desert, the forty days of the flood, and particularly forty as a number of trials and crossings.
G5062.emploi: The word appears about 20 times in the New Testament, present in all four Gospels and especially in Acts, Revelation, and the Epistles. It designates both concrete durations (the forty days of Jesus' fast in Matthew 4:2, Mark 1:13, and Luke 4:2), historical periods (the forty years of Israel in the desert reported in Acts with reference to the Old Testament), and enumerated quantities (the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem measured in cubits in Revelation 21:17). In all cases, the number retains its biblical symbolic charge: a period of trial, purification, or waiting.
G5062.portee: Forty reminds us that God does not abandon his people to the difficulties of the desert; the forty years are not a senseless punishment, but a time of training and maturation. When Jesus fasts for forty days, he recapitulates Israel's experience and triumphs where Israel has faltered. This number invites the reader to see in trial and waiting a work of God that purifies faith.

sens: age of forty completed years
duration of a period of forty years
G5063.detail:
1. This word designates the precise age of forty years: Moses was forty years old when he decided to visit his Israelite brothers (Acts 7:23). It is the Greek expression to indicate that one has reached this age.
2. More broadly, it also designates a complete period or duration of forty years: God fed the Israelites for forty years in the desert (Acts 13:18), which shows the fulfillment of an entire generation's journey to the promised land.
G5063.origine: The word is composed of the root that designates the number forty (tessarakonta) and the suffix -etēs which indicates age or duration in years. It is a classical Greek formation to express age or periodicity: the same suffix is found in other expressions of duration or age.
G5063.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts. It first occurs when Luke mentions that Moses had reached his forty years (Acts 7:23), a pivotal moment in his life when he chooses to identify his fate with that of his oppressed people. It then appears regarding the forty years that God granted the people in the desert (Acts 13:18), recalling the symbolic duration of trial and discipline in the desert before entering the Promised Land. These two uses show that forty years marks a decisive turning point or a complete cycle in the history of salvation.
G5063.portee: These two moments — Moses at forty ready to free his people, and forty years of wandering in the desert — remind the reader that God orders time according to his plans. Forty years is not an insignificant number in the Bible: it is a period of transition, purification, and maturation. These passages invite the believer to recognize that God acts according to his timetable and that a time may prove necessary to accomplish his purpose.

sens: the number 4
a group of four people or four things
the four directions or cardinal points
G5064.detail:
1. The number four itself, used for counting: John 19:23 mentions the four parts of Jesus' garments divided among the soldiers, and Acts 21:23 speaks of four men who have made a vow.
2. A group of four entities: Revelation 4:4 describes the twenty-four elders worshiping God, and Revelation 4:6 mentions the four living creatures around the throne, celestial beings with symbolic function.
3. The four corners of the earth or the four cardinal points, expressing universality or totality: Matthew 24:31 speaks of gathering the elect from the "four winds" (that is, from all directions of the world), and Revelation 7:1 evokes "the four winds of the earth," symbols of the forces that control the universe.
G5064.origine: The Greek word tessares comes from an ancient Indo-European root designating this number. In Hebrew, the number four is called arba, which shares the same distant origin. The number four often has a biblical symbolic charge: it designates the four corners or extremities of creation (the four winds, the four horns of an altar), thus marking exhaustiveness or totality, while in Revelation it structures the heavenly visions (four living creatures, twenty-four elders).
G5064.emploi: The word appears about 35 times in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in Revelation (over 20 occurrences), where the number four organizes the visions: four living creatures, four horns, four winds. It is also found in the Gospels for concrete facts (four parts of garments in John 19:23, four men in Acts 21:23) and to express universality (the four winds in Matthew 24:31). The number carries a cosmic and symbolic meaning in apocalyptic texts: it represents the order of creation and its total extent.
G5064.portee: The number four, particularly in Revelation, reinforces the idea that God governs the entirety of the universe and history. When we see the four living creatures or the four winds, we understand that God's purpose extends everywhere, without limit. This reassures the persecuted believer: no force in the world escapes God's control, and his salvation is destined for all regions of the earth.

sens: which comes in the fourteenth rank in an ordered series
G5065.detail: 1. This word designates the number fourteen in an order, a succession. In Acts 27:27, Paul and his companions have been at sea for fourteen nights during the storm that drives their ship toward the shore. In Acts 27:33, Paul speaks of the fourteenth day they spend without eating, in waiting and fear. It is simply an ordinal number that counts a position in time.
G5065.origine: The Greek word comes from two parts: "tessares" (four) and "dekatos" (tenth), combined to form "fourteenth." It is a simple and transparent composition of ancient Greek for ordinal numbers beyond ten: ten plus four equals fourteen.
G5065.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, and only in Acts 27, the account of Paul's shipwreck on the way to Rome. Both uses occur in the same dramatic context: first for the night of the fourteenth day of the storm, then for the day itself when provisions run out. The word is used simply to establish the chronology of events and emphasize the duration of this trial.
G5065.portee: This temporal detail reminds us that the Christian faith is lived in the concrete: Paul goes through challenging days, counted one by one, without knowing when deliverance will come. For the Christian reader, this shows that trust in God is manifested when one endures, day after day, without seeing the end.

sens: Concerning the fourth day
Who has been dead for four days
G5066.detail:
1. This word describes what belongs to or relates to the fourth day. It is an adjective formed from the number four: it qualifies something that occurs or exists on the fourth day of a sequence.
2. In its unique biblical usage, the word concretely means "since four days ago." Jesus arrives in Bethany and learns that Lazarus has been dead for four days: Martha tells Jesus, "He stinks already, for he has been there four days" (John 11:39). The adjective emphasizes the elapsed time, the decomposition of the body, and prepares for the extraordinary miracle of resurrection.
G5066.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective τέταρτος (tétartos), which means "fourth." It is derived from the number four (τέσσαρες, tessares). The form τεταρταῖος adds a nuance of duration or state: it does not simply say "the fourth" but "that which lasts four days" or "of the fourth day." This type of formation is characteristic of Greek to express a position in a series with an idea of time that passes.
G5066.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 11:39, during the resurrection of Lazarus. Martha uses the expression "he is of the fourth day" (literally "he is four days dead") to signal to Jesus that the body has begun to decompose. This detail underscores the expectation and impatience of the disciples and the sisters, as well as the absolute certainty that Lazarus is dead. The number four days, far from being trivial, carries theological significance: in Jewish tradition, the soul was believed to remain near the body for three days; the fourth day marked the point of no return from death.
G5066.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus only raises Lazarus when all human hope is lost and death has seemingly won its victory. It is when Lazarus has been in the tomb for four days that Jesus manifests His power and total dominion over death. For the reader, this detail reinforces faith: the miracle is unequivocal, doubt is not possible.

sens: which comes after the third in an order or succession
which constitutes an equal part when dividing something into four
G5067.detail:
1. This word simply designates what occupies the fourth position in a series or enumeration. In the fourth watch of the night (Matthew 14:25), it refers to the last third of the night, divided into four watches by the Romans. In Revelation, the fourth living creature (Revelation 4:7) follows the lion, the calf, and the one with the face of a man in the vision. Similarly, the fourth seal (Revelation 6:7) is opened after the first three in the succession of judgments.
2. The word also takes on the meaning of part or portion when it qualifies a fraction: in Revelation 6:8, it refers to a quarter of the earth, that is, a portion divided into four equal parts. The context shows that this measures the power of death and Hades over a limited part of creation.
G5067.origine: The word comes from the Greek root that expresses the number four. It is a regular adjective formed to indicate rank or order. In both Greek and French, ordinal numbers (first, second, third, fourth…) allow for the classification and counting of elements in a series. The Hebrew of the Old Testament uses the same type of form (רְבִיעִי, "fourth") for the same usage.
G5067.emploi: This word appears nine times in the New Testament, mostly in Luke (Acts) and John (Revelation). It is primarily used to mark a position in an enumeration: the four living creatures of the vision in Revelation, the four seals, or the four watches of the Roman night. In Revelation 6:8, it loses its strict ordinal meaning to designate a fraction (the quarter), showing that the word can express both order and division. In Acts 10:30, the expression "four days" (literally "since four days") simply counts a time interval.
G5067.portee: This simple word reminds us of the importance of numbers in biblical narration: the visions of Revelation organize the cosmos into sets of four (the living creatures, the horsemen) to express the completeness of creation and the order of divine judgment. For the believer, seeing how God structures His revelations in complete series invites recognition of a coherent and determined plan in the history of the world.

sens: In shape with four equal sides and four right angles
Having equal surface or volume on each face
G5068.detail:
1. The word describes the simplest geometric shape: a figure with four sides of equal length and four right angles. In Revelation 21:16, the heavenly city is presented as a perfect square, whose length equals its width; the verse even specifies that the height is also equal, forming a cube, a symbol of divine harmony and perfection.
2. In an extended sense, the word can qualify an object having this shape in all its dimensions. This geometric perfection evokes in the Bible completeness and order, contrasting with the disorder of the current world.
G5068.origine: The Greek word tetragōnos is composed of tetra-, meaning "four," and gonia, meaning "angle." Literally: "having four angles." This transparent construction allows the Greek reader to immediately understand the described shape. The word translates the biblical Hebrew idea of rectangular or square shape (root rabá').
G5068.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in the apocalyptic vision of John describing the New Jerusalem. The use of the term "square" (and more broadly the image of a perfect cube when adding height) emphasizes the absolute symmetry and divine order of the heavenly city. The revealing context of John 21 shows that geometry is not just a detail here: it expresses justice, perfection, and the immutability of God's eternal dwelling with men.
G5068.portee: For the reader, this word paints an image of future divine perfection. The city of God is not irregular or lopsided: it is of perfect symmetry, reassuring the Christian about the order and justice that will reign in eternity. This perfect geometry reminds us that God creates and will arrange all things in righteousness and harmony.

sens: group of four soldiers
basic military unit in the Roman army
detachment assigned to guard a prisoner
G5069.detail:
1. A squad of four is literally a group of four soldiers forming a small unit. In Acts 12:4, Herod puts Peter in prison and assigns him to the guard of four squads of four soldiers each — a total of sixteen soldiers — to keep a close watch on him until the day of Passover.
2. This is a common Roman military organization: four men constitute a team that can show guard continuously, each taking turns to remain vigilant while the others rest. This division into four allows for uninterrupted surveillance during the four parts of the night.
3. The word thus also designates the role of this team: to guard, to watch over, to maintain security. The presence of four squads shows the importance that political power placed on capturing Peter and the concern over his reputed powers.
G5069.origine: The Greek word tetradion comes from the root tetra, meaning "four." It is a diminutive: it specifically designates a small group of four, not just the number four. The word is formed on the model of Greek and Latin military terms for organized units. It reflects the Roman military system, where soldiers were grouped into teams of various sizes according to needs.
G5069.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 12:4. Luke uses it in the narrator's voice to describe how Herod Agrippa arranges his army to guard Peter after his arrest. The context shows that Peter was considered a prisoner of very high importance — four groups of four soldiers, thus a particularly reinforced and permanent presence. This historical detail reflects Roman security practices.
G5069.portee: This passage reminds us that even in the face of the most organized political and military powers, the early church does not depend on its own strength. A few verses later, an angel miraculously frees Peter from this prison guarded by sixteen soldiers. The word "squad" emphasizes the futility of all these human preparations in the face of divine intervention.

sens: Number equal to four times one thousand, that is, four thousand units
G5070.detail: 1. This word simply designates the number 4,000. In the Gospels, it appears in the account of the multiplication of the loaves: Jesus feeds four thousand people with a few loaves and small fish (Matthew 15:38, Mark 8:9). It represents a large number of people gathered to listen to Jesus and receive his teaching. The word is also used to count the Egyptian rebels that a Roman officer confuses with the apostle Paul (Acts 21:38).
G5070.origine: The Greek word is formed from τετράκι (four times) and χίλιοι (thousand). It is a compound numeral adjective that simply reproduces the multiplication 4 × 1,000. Ancient Greek has specialized words to express large numbers accurately.
G5070.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the New Testament, always to designate a significant crowd. Three passages report the miracle of the multiplication of the loaves (Matthew 15:38, 16:10, Mark 8:9, 8:20), where Jesus feeds four thousand men, not counting women and children. One passage reports that the Roman officer Lysias confuses Paul with "that Egyptian who recently stirred up a revolt and led four thousand assassins into the wilderness" (Acts 21:38). In all cases, the number emphasizes the exceptional scale of the event.
G5070.portee: This number reminds the reader of the extent of Jesus' power: he provides food for a multitude without ordinary means. It is a visible sign of his compassion and authority over creation. For the believer, it is an invitation to trust Jesus even when resources seem insufficient.

sens: The number 400
G5071.detail: 1. This Greek word simply designates the number four hundred. It is found in the New Testament to express quantities or durations: about four hundred men followed Theudas (Acts 5:36), the descendants of Abraham were to stay in captivity for four hundred years (Acts 7:6), God gave judges to Israel for about four hundred and fifty years (Acts 13:20), and the law came four hundred and thirty years after the promise made to Abraham (Galatians 3:17).
G5071.origine: The Greek word τετρακόσιοι is composed of τέτρα- ("four") and κόσιοι ("hundreds"). It is a cardinal numeral adjective that functions like all numbers in Greek. The structure of the word simply reflects the combination of the two elements: four (tétra-) and hundred (-cosioi).
G5071.emploi: This word appears only four times in the New Testament, always in Acts and the epistle to the Galatians. Its uses are exclusively numerical: it serves to quantify men (the followers of Theudas) or to express historical periods (the four hundred years of captivity in Egypt, the four hundred and fifty years of the period of the judges, the four hundred and thirty years between the promise and the law). In each context, the number emphasizes an important duration or magnitude in the history of salvation.
G5071.portee: These four occurrences refer to major milestones in sacred history: the captivity in Egypt, the periods of Israel before the monarchy, and the interval between the promise to Abraham and the Law at Sinai. For the Christian reader, these long durations remind us of God's patience in fulfilling his promises and the persistence of his people through trials. It is a call to see how God guides human history according to his plan.

sens: Time period equal to about one hundred twenty days, or one third of a year
Figuratively, a delay or lapse of time considered long or significant
G5072.detail:
1. The word literally designates a duration of four consecutive months. Jesus uses it in John 4:35 to speak of the time remaining until the harvest: "Do you not say that there are still four months until the harvest?" It is a way of measuring time by the seasons and agricultural work, concrete for his listeners.

2. Beyond the simple measure of time, the expression evokes a delay that may seem long to the one who waits. By using this duration, Jesus emphasizes that the spiritual harvest is already visible and does not require much longer: the wait is shorter than generally believed.
G5072.origine: The word is composed of τέσσαρα (four) and μήνη (month): literally "four-months." It is a classical Greek adjective formed transparently. In Hebrew, there is an equivalent structure with "four months" (עַרְבָּעָה חֳדָשִׁים) in the Greek Old Testament, for example in Judges 19:2. The word belongs to the ordinary vocabulary of measuring time.
G5072.emploi: This word appears only once in John 4:35, in the context where Jesus teaches his disciple the Samaritan woman and his disciples. He uses this temporal reference to dramatize his point: there are not four months until the harvest, but behold, the fields are already white for harvest. It is a teaching moment where Jesus speaks of the spiritual harvest as a present, imminent reality, not a future one. The choice of the word showed an agrarian audience that they understood the language of seasons and the work of the land.
G5072.portee: For the Christian reader, this verse invites consideration of the urgency of the mission and the spiritual harvest: God does not ask for a long wait. The image of the whitening harvest speaks to every generation of believers, who must see the present opportunity and not postpone to tomorrow what God puts before their eyes today.

sens: which is worth four times as much
which is multiplied by four
G5073.detail:
1. The word designates what is four times larger or worth four times as much. It is a compound word: "tetra" means four, and "ploos" means multiplied by. Zacchaeus promises to repay fourfold what he has taken from someone (Luke 19:8): if someone has been defrauded of one hundred denarii, Zacchaeus will return four hundred.
2. By extension, this expresses a generous and abundant restitution, well beyond what would simply be just. In repaying four times the amount, Zacchaeus is not only seeking to make amends but to overcompensate, demonstrating the sincerity of his conversion.
G5073.origine: The word comes from two Greek elements: "tetra" which means four (found in "tetramorph," composed of four forms) and "ploos" which means times or multiplied by. It is a classical compound adjective in Greek.
G5073.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke (19:8). It is found in the account of Zacchaeus, the tax collector from Jericho who encounters Jesus. Zacchaeus, recognizing his injustices, commits to repaying fourfold all that he has extorted through fraud. This quadruple restitution was in accordance with the Old Testament law for certain types of damages (for example, Exodus 22:1 for livestock theft), which shows that Zacchaeus accepts the strictest standards of justice.
G5073.portee: This word reveals how conversion concretely transforms the heart and actions. Zacchaeus does not merely believe in Jesus; he generously restores, exceeding what is owed. For the reader, this shows that an encounter with Jesus produces authentic generosity and justice, surpassing the minimum requirement of the law.

sens: Animal with four legs
Terrestrial creature in a listing of living beings
G5074.detail:
1. The word literally designates any animal that moves on four legs. In the vision that Peter receives in Acts 10:12, he sees a sheet filled with quadrupeds (along with reptiles and birds), which foreshadows the announcement that foods once declared unclean according to the Law can be received by Christians.

2. The word also appears in the parallel passage of Acts 11:6, where Peter recounts the same vision, and in Romans 1:23, where Paul describes how men distant from God worshiped images of quadrupeds instead of the living God. In these three contexts, quadrupeds are among the terrestrial creatures: sometimes in a neutral enumeration of the animal world, sometimes to show how all of creation, including beasts, was once at the service of idolatrous worship.
G5074.origine: The word comes from the Greek tettara (four) and pous (foot). It is a simple and transparent compound: one who has four feet. In Hebrew, the term behem (beast) is used, which is broader and covers all quadrupeds and large domesticated animals.
G5074.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the three provided passages. It is used to designate animals walking on four legs, in contrast to birds (which fly) and reptiles (which crawl). The first occurrence is in Peter's vision, which becomes a turning point in Christian ministry by lifting Jewish dietary barriers. The other two occurrences reiterate or illustrate this same reality.
G5074.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that Peter's vision marks a decisive moment: the Gospel is opened to non-Jews. By seeing unclean quadrupeds in the heavenly sheet that God lowers, Peter understands that what God has declared clean must not be rejected—a lesson that applies to all peoples. The word also shows how every creature exists within God's order, and how serious it is for man to worship an image of a quadruped rather than the Creator Himself.

sens: exercising the political authority of a tetrarch, that is, ruling over a quarter of territory or a region
G5075.detail: 1. Being a tetrarch means to govern a territory or region as a prince or governor: the Greek word is composed of 'four' and 'to rule', but it practically designates a political leader who rules over an administrative district of the Roman Empire, without being a king in the full sense. At the time John the Baptist preaches, Herod (the son of the great king Herod) is tetrarch of Galilee, while his brother Philip is tetrarch of Iturea and the region of Trachonitis (Luke 3:1): this title shows their subordinate status to Rome, less prestigious than that of a king, but real.
G5075.origine: The word comes from the Greek: 'tetra' means 'four' and 'archè' means 'to rule' or 'to command'. Originally, the title designated one who commanded a quarter of a territory divided among four leaders. The word is formed on the same root as 'archangel' (one who commands angels) or 'monarch' (one who rules alone).
G5075.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:1. Luke uses it to provide the political and religious context of John the Baptist's preaching: by mentioning the different leaders who rule at that time (Pontius Pilate, Herod, Philip, Lysanias), he shows the political division of the Holy Land under Roman domination and situates the event in contemporary history.
G5075.portee: This word helps us understand the political context of the ministry of Jesus and John the Baptist: the region was fragmented among several human authorities. It reminds us that Jesus grew up under the rule of Herod Antipas, a tetrarch dependent on Rome, and announces that His kingdom was of another nature—not political and earthly, but eternal and spiritual.

sens: One who governs a quarter of a region
Small sovereign or prince of lower rank
In the case of Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, governor of Galilee and Transjordan
G5076.detail:
1. The word originally designates a military chief or administrator who controls a fraction of a territory—literally 'one who rules over four parts'. It is a title of lower rank than that of king: a tetrarch often depends on a higher authority.
2. More broadly, it applies to any small sovereign or prince possessing limited authority over a restricted domain, without the power of a king.
3. In the Gospel, the word specifically designates Herod Antipas, the younger son of Herod the Great. After the death of his father, the empire was divided among his sons: Antipas received Galilee and Transjordan (Perea), hence his title of tetrarch (Matthew 14:1). He is the one who had John the Baptist killed (Luke 3:19) and to whom Jesus was sent during His Passion.
G5076.origine: The Greek word combines two elements: 'tetra-' (four) and 'archéin' (to command, to rule). The starting image is that of command over four parts of a whole. It is a compound analogous to 'monarch' (one king) or 'oligarch' (a few who rule). The word has retained this precise administrative meaning in the Greco-Roman world.
G5076.emploi: The term appears only 4 times in the New Testament, always in the Gospels and Acts, and always to designate Herod Antipas. Matthew 14:1 presents him as the one who heard about Jesus and thought it was John the Baptist raised from the dead. Luke 3:19 recalls that Antipas the tetrarch had John the Baptist arrested because of Herodias and her crimes. In Luke 9:7, Herod the tetrarch is perplexed upon hearing about the deeds of Jesus. In Acts 13:1, Manaen had been brought up with the tetrarch, showing the importance of this political figure in the Levant. The title emphasizes his limited authority in the context of Roman power.
G5076.portee: For the reader, the word reminds us that Jesus did not operate in a political vacuum, but in a real world subject to small potentates jealous of their power. Herod Antipas embodies the anxious prince, easily influenced by fear and intrigue (he fears Jesus, he kills John the Baptist under the pressure of Herodias). This word also shows the humble administrative condition of the territory where Jesus exercised His ministry: neither a great empire nor an independent kingdom, but a region governed by a second-rank official.

sens: Completely burn something until it is transformed into ash
Destroy by fire in a total and irreversible manner
G5077.detail:
1. The verb literally means to turn into ashes, that is, to burn something so intensely and completely that only gray powder remains. The image is one of destruction by fire that annihilates all structure: in 2 Peter 2:6, the apostle describes how God reduced the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes, completely consuming these cities by divine judgment.
2. Figuratively, the word expresses the total and definitive destruction of a thing—here entire cities with their inhabitants—by a superior power, here that of God. It is an act of judgment that leaves nothing intact: the ashes become the visible sign that sin has been radically condemned and annihilated.
G5077.origine: The word comes from the Greek τέφρα (téphra), which means 'ash'—the gray powder that remains after an intense fire. The verb is formed with the suffix -οω which creates a verb from a noun. Ash is essentially what remains of complete destruction, the ultimate residue of fire: the word thus evokes total annihilation, to the end.
G5077.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:6. Peter uses it to describe God's judgment on Sodom and Gomorrah—two biblical cities emblematic of sin and rebellion against God. By reducing them to ashes, God transformed them into a warning, a visible example for all the ungodly to come. This verb emphasizes the intensity and irreversibility of divine judgment: it is not a partial destruction, but complete annihilation.
G5077.portee: This word reminds the reader that God's judgment on sin is real, total, and final. The ruins of Sodom and Gomorrah reduced to ashes are not a fable: they are a concrete warning for all those who reject God. For the Christian, this passage invites us to take seriously the holiness of God and the gravity of sin, while reconnecting us to the grace of God that offers an escape through Christ.

sens: know-how, skill acquired in a particular field
trade, professional activity that requires training
creative or technical work that produces a work
industry, commerce based on a trade or craft
G5078.detail:
1. The word technē primarily refers to know-how, the skill acquired through learning and practice: it is the ability of the tent maker or the sculptor who masters his field (Acts 18:3: Paul had the same trade as Priscilla and Aquila, the making of tents).
2. By extension, technē refers to the trade itself, the profession practiced: Revelation 18:22 mentions all the craftsmen of trades in the great city, all those who live by their know-how.
3. The word also applies to art in the sense of creation: Acts 17:29 speaks of statuettes "sculpted by the art and craft of man," where technē refers to the creative work of the sculptor.
4. Finally, technē can evoke the entirety of commercial activity based on these trades: Revelation 18:22 describes the economic ruin of a city where all trades and artisanal work disappear.
G5078.origine: The word technē comes from an Indo-European root meaning "to make" or "to build." It is related to the idea of shaping something with intelligence and skill. The Greek word evokes the progressive learning of a skill: one who masters a technē has acquired a practical knowledge that can be transmitted. In the Greek Old Testament, technē translates notably חׇכְמָה (practical wisdom), מַעֲשֶׂה (work, fabrication), and עֲבֹדָה (work), all of which evoke a useful and concrete know-how.
G5078.emploi: The word technē appears only three times in the New Testament. It first refers to the trade of tent maker (Acts 18:3), illustrating a precise and recognized professional skill. In Acts 17:29, it describes the work of the sculptor who creates idols, the technical art serving creation. In Revelation 18:22, it more broadly refers to all trades and all craftsmen, suggesting how the ruin of a city takes with it all its economic and artisanal activity. The word remains always concrete: it never designates an abstraction, but always an applied know-how, a trade, a productive activity.
G5078.portee: This word reminds us that manual and artisanal work has value in the eyes of God. Paul, apostle of Jesus Christ, does not hesitate to practice a trade (the making of tents) to live and preach the Gospel: there is dignity in craftsmanship and in the work of his hands. Revelation 18:22 also warns us that if the economy of a society rests entirely on commerce separated from God, that society is heading for ruin: even the most necessary trades will disappear with it.

sens: One who makes something with their hands, possessing a particular skill
One who practices a craft or technical trade
One who designs and builds, like an architect or master builder
G5079.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a man who makes objects with his hands with acquired skill — an artisan in the most concrete sense. In Acts 19:24, Demetrius is a silversmith who makes miniature temples in silver: he is a skilled worker who masters an art, the transformation of materials. The term thus evokes someone who possesses a particular technique and practices it to earn a living.
2. More broadly, it designates one who practices any trade — carpenter, blacksmith, potter, musician. In Revelation 18:22, God laments the disappearance of "every craftsman of any trade": it is the entirety of human trades and skills that vanish.
3. The word can also refer to one who designs and builds, in the sense of architect or master builder. In Hebrews 11:10, God is called "the architect and builder" of the heavenly city: He is the intelligent creator and builder of it.
G5079.origine: The word comes from the root τέχνη (technique, art, skill). A τεχνίτης is therefore literally one who possesses and practices a technique, a skill. In Hebrew from the Old Testament, this word translates notably חָרָשׁ (harash), which means artisan or skilled worker. The Greek word always emphasizes the idea of competence and acquired mastery, not just manual labor.
G5079.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, three times in the concrete sense of skilled worker, once in a figurative sense. In Acts 19:24-38, Demetrius and his workers are artisans who live from making small temples; they fear that Paul's preaching will destroy their business.
